speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I wish to inform the House that pursuant to the order of the House adopted on Monday, January 21, 1991, and the provisions of Standing Order 28(3), I sent a notice calling the House to meet this day, and I now lay this notice on the Table.
In addition, on Thursday, February 21, 1991, I sent each member a message by electronic mail explaining the reasons for calling back the House.

I also wish to inform the House that in accordance with the representation made by the government under the provisions of Standing Order 55(1), I have caused to be published a special Order Paper giving notices of a government motion and of a government bill.

I also wish to lay on the Table a letter from the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, dated Wednesday, February 20, 1991.

subsubtopic: THE LATE CLAYTON D'ENTREMONT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 14 the inshore ground fishery in southwestern Nova Scotia lost a pillar and a tireless advocate
in the fisheries when Clayton d'Entremont of Meteghan and West Pubnico was killed in a car accident at the age of 38.
I knew Clayton well, Mr. Speaker, and I was always impressed with the depth of his commitment to the cause of independent fishermen and processors. During a time when a strong voice was needed for the inshore, Clayton was always there making the best case he could on countless fishery advisory committees.
People of the quality of Clayton are rare these days, Mr. Speaker. That we should lose someone like him now, when our country faces so many challenges at home and abroad, is sadder still. The consistency of his commitment to a cause should be an example to us all.
To his wife, Roberta, his daughter, Lauren, and his family, I extend my sincerest condolences. It was an honour to have worked with Clayton for so many years. The fishing community of southwestern Nova Scotia will miss him.

Mr. Speaker, the reins of government in Nova Scotia are about to be transferred from one farmer to another farmer. Premier Roger Bacon will step down after serving six months as premier of the province and although the position as premier was an interim position, Mr. Bacon did far more than an interim job. By the time that his term was up he had impressed the people of Nova Scotia and the people of all the Atlantic provinces with his ability. Roger Bacon did an outstanding job in a very difficult situation.
Soon another dairy farmer takes over. The Hon. Donald Cameron will become the first native of Pictou County to become premier of our province. Mr. Cameron brings with him a reputation of honesty and integrity as well as 16 years as an MLA and minister in the Nova Scotia legislature.

February 25, 1991
Nova Scotians look forward to his frank leadership style and are optimistic about the future under his government which will be sworn in tomorrow, February 26.
Congratulations and good luck to Mr. Cameron and his government.

Mr. Speaker, Saskatchewan's plans to harmonize its retail sales tax with the federal government's GST is just one more example of cheerleadering and Premier Grant Devine's dancing to the Prime Minister's tune.
For our premier, who once said he opposed the GST, to agree not only to collect this harmful and regressive tax, but also to tiy to take $200 million annually out of the Saskatchewan economy for his own purposes is shameful. Less than four months ago, after much thought, he said, the premier announced the GST would be introduced "side by side" with the provincial tax and Saskatchewan businesses prepared their records and equipment to accommodate this.
Now, with the demand for a federal agriculture payment looming, Devine changes his mind and all that business planning and expense have gone for naught. The people of Saskatchewan know there is a provincial election coming. I remind the Saskatchewan voter that we wanted to say no to the federal GST) we will soon get a chance to say no to Devine's GST.

Mr. Speaker, the Quebec mining association strenuously objects to the proposed amendments to the Financial Administration Act regarding cost recovery in the marine and air freight sectors.
These additional expenses and costs, especially in the marine sector, will have a disastrous impact on the economy of certain regions, especially in the mining industry. Cost recovery will mean additional expenditures which companies will be unable to recover from the
customer, who can find other suppliers on the international market.
Instead of opting for additional charges, the federal government should consider implementing recent recommendations by the Auditor General of Canada, which suggested cutting costs and privatizing certain services to save money, instead of putting an additional burden on Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, reform of the Public Service of Canada is supposedly proceeding under the program known as Public Service 2000. Announced in December 1989, the stated objective of Public Service 2000 "is to enable the Public Service to provide the best possible service to Canadians into the 21st century".
But so far, Public Service 2000 has succeeded mainly in alienating thousands of public servants. Public Service 2000 has forsaken employee consultation. There has been no parliamentary or public debate on this issue, despite repeated requests from Liberal MPS and Public Service unions in general. The 24,000-member Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada boycotted a National Joint Council meeting last fall as a form of protest because of this cavalier attitude.
If thousands of public servants are not being consulted, and their concerns not considered, how can the government expect this reform to succeed? The Conservative government is missing the opportunity for meaningful consultation with public servants, Parliament and the Canadian public.
I deplore the lack of sensitivity of this government in matters of the Public Service of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just came back from a short trip to Haiti as a member of the Canadian delegation to the swearing-in of Father Jean Bertrand Aristide.
The election held on December 16 in that country has given people hope for the future and helped them break

with a past history of dictatorship, violence and corruption. They can now aspire to democracy and progress.
The Haitian people, so rich in history-their country became the first independent black State in 1804-but poor in economic resources, need Canada's development aid. This aid should be substantially increased, considering the ties between our two countries. More than 60,000 Haitians live in Canada, mostly in Quebec, and Haiti is a member of the international francophone community.
I am convinced that my government will respond to this appeal from a country that has so much to offer and does so with pride and dignity.

Mr. Speaker, the World Food Program predicts that in 1991, 25 African countries will face a food shortage of 4 million tonnes, affecting 30 million people. The gulf war is endangering humanitarian aid to these African countries by diverting world attention and emergency funding away from this famine.
What are Canada's priorities relative to the gulf war and the need to help feed the world's starving people? Canada should not be more supportive of offensive military action in the gulf than it is to saving lives in Africa and throughout the developing world.
Tomorrow's federal budget will be Canada's opportunity to clearly state its priorities. Will we increase our commitment to emergency aid and development assistance now, when it is needed most and while the world's attention is focused elsewhere? If we do, we will be showing that Canadians believe that the saving of lives is a priority over all else.

Mr. Speaker, more and more Canadians every day are expressing interest and concern about the future of our country. Many are taking advantage of the citizens' forum and its process to get involved in planning the future of Canada. I would like to bring to the attention of the House and
the government the recent initiative of the Lunenburg Board of Trade, which has established a committee to respond to the challenge of the forum.
In a recent letter to me, which I would be pleased to share with all members of the House, the committee totally rejected the notion that Atlantic Canada should be cut off from the rest of Canada. They urge all Canadians, particularly the separatists of Quebec, not to assume that separation would mean the geographic isolation of Atlantic Canada.
They further, and quite properly, urge all Canadians to give pro-active consideration to the basis upon which we can build a new confederation, one which preserves the strengths of Canada today while responding to the legitimate cultural and regional interests as well.

Mr. Speaker, all Canadians have been affected by this government's slashing of the CBC, but none as severely as Atlantic Canadians. The recent cuts are responsible for the cancellation of the highest rated series produced by the CBC in this country, Land and Sea.
Land and Sea is a maritime tradition. It is distinctive to the Atlantic region. No other program covers the cares and concerns of this area better than Land and Sea. All Atlantic Canadians believe it is crucial to have some understanding of what drives the region economically, of the traditions and values that make us unique. It is, therefore, crucial that we have an opportunity to appreciate the beauty of our region and the importance of our resources and have this interpreted on our public television system.
We are not asking for something new and we are not placing an unfair burden on government. Atlantic Canadians only want to see Land and Sea back on the screen.
I know that this government must stay at arms length from programming decisions, however, the elimination of Land and Sea should be of concern to any government. A recommendation from this government or an acknowledgement of how vital this program is to the Atlantic region might maintain our 20 year old tradition.

February 25, 1991
On behalf of Atlantic Canadians, I ask this government to speak out for Land and Sea.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after Manchuria in 1931, Abyssinia in 1935 and World War II where 40 million people died brutally, the UN was created with the intention and power to stop bullies when they attacked other countries and killed innocent people. Unfortunately, for 40 years the cold war blocked collective action.
In the case of Saddam Hussein's attack on Kuwait, the UN acted unitedly and with great courage for sanctions and then action. Canada was part of that collective and courageous decision. The Liberals and NDP were opposed.
A few days ago Saddam Hussein made an offer to withdraw which had so many conditions that he would still have an aggressive capacity and intention. The Liberals and NDP wanted to accept his very first offer. The government and the UN coalition properly rejected this offer.
The bottom line is that neither the Liberal Party nor the New Democratic Party are worthy to govern Canada with our proud tradition of supporting the UN and its many agencies.

Mr. Speaker, with the exception of this government, everyone agrees that high interest rates and the high Canadian dollar are decimating Canadian manufacturing industry. If you want a concrete example, try Algoma Steel.
What we require now are assurances, a guarantee that the Americans will not construe a loan guarantee as a subsidy and slap us with a countervail duty. It is not enough to speak to Canadian legal counsel. We must go directly to our American counterparts in steel, trade and the government.
The Minister of Industry, Science and Technology assured me that he would be a part of a task force to study the long-term viability of Algoma. In an ensuing press conference, he indicated that there was no way that
the federal government would involve itself in the long-term restructuring of Algoma.
The government is part of the problem and it must be part of the solution. The minister must be an active participant, not a spectator in the task force.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was quite a week for Calgary swimmer Mark Tewksbury. Capacity crowds at the Lindsay Park Sports Centre cheered Mark on to three world records. The University of Calgary Swim Club sprinter set the new world records in the 50, 100 and 200 metres backstroke.
Canadians will be watching proudly as Mark takes on the world's best at the World Cup in Europe next month. He is now the one to beat.
Congratulations, Mark, and good luck.

Mr. Speaker, over the past few weeks I have received calls, letters and petitions from seniors throughout the province of Manitoba and especially from my own constituency, the federal constituency of St. Boniface.
I have received more than 400 such statements from one centre, the St. Vital Senior Centre, asking that I, with my Liberal colleagues, do everything in our power to restore Canada's universal health care program, which the government is systematically dismantling through legislation such as Bill C-69. Collectively we must stop and we will stop the government's attempts to eliminate the federal role in health care. These actions, such as Bill C-69, could lead to eventual privatization of our excellent health care system which exists for all Canadians and could become the preserve of the rich only.
Canada's health care act assures no user fees, no extra billing by doctors and universality.

If the government decides to tackle the health program tomorrow, if it keeps on attacking our seniors, I can assure you it will have a fight on its hands!

Mr. Speaker, I know that all members of this House will join me in wishing the Leader of the Opposition a speedy recovery.

Our thoughts and prayers are with the Chretien family.

My question is for the Prime Minister. After six and a half years of Conservative government, our country has never been in worse shape, economically or constitutionally. After an election campaign promising jobs, jobs, jobs, will the Prime Minister explain why 1.3 million Canadians have no jobs, why 186,000 Canadian children line up at food banks every month, why 54,000 Canadian bankruptcies were declared last year and why our competitive position vis-a-vis the United States is the worst that it has been in 40 years.
Did the Prime Minister deliberately cause a national recession, or did he just mismanage the economy into one?

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised at the comparisons that the hon. member has drawn. She says that the economy has never been in worse shape since the 1930s. She has a very short memory because it was in awful lot worse shape in the 1981-1982 recession-
Hear, hear.

-and that no one would disagree with.
The hon. member talks about the level of bankruptcies. If she would care to look behind the bankruptcy figures-which no one is happy about-she would see that, according to The Financial Post today, there are 160,000 business formations per year. The small business association, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, say it is as high as 340,000 new businesses that are created. I think that is the important factor.
Oral Questions
We on this side of the House are not happy about the fact that the economy is in a recession and we are doing everything we can to get the economy out of recession, and I will have more to say about that tomorrow in my budget.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side remember what the minister said. He said you have to die before you go to heaven, and right now there are 1.3 million Canadians dying for some new jobs.

As a result of the GST, 80,000 Canadian men and women lost their jobs in the service sector in the month of January alone. As a result of the government's policies, 300,000 Canadians lost their jobs in the manufacturing sector during the past two years.
What specific policies will the minister announce tomorrow that will give a measure of hope to those thousands and thousands of unemployed workers who are waiting for answers from the government?
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member would wait until tomorrow, she could have a good answer to that question.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative government has mismanaged trade, mismanaged the dollar, mismanaged interest rates, mismanaged taxes, and mismanaged the national debt which this minister in his predictions of 1984 predicted would be at $18 billion in 1991.
Despite seven years of incredible world-wide growth, Canada is in the grips of a vicious recession.
Does the Prime Minister realize that his agenda of favouring the rich, hammering the middle class, and ignoring the poor is killing Canada's economy?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend persists in talking about 1981-82. In 1981-82 we had interest rates that were 22 per cent and 23 per cent. Interest rates today are in the 9 per cent to 10 per cent range.
She talks about unemployment. Unemployment then was 14 per cent, the peak of unemployment. We have an unemployment rate that is just short of 10 per cent today. The level of inflation hit 13 per cent. Today we

February 25, 1991
Oral Questions
have an underlying inflation rate that is around 4 per cent.
My hon. friend is falling into a major trap. She should not be trying to use these tactics of comparing today with one of the blackest moments in our economic history of 1981-1982 and expect to come out unscathed.

Mr. Speaker, for the more than 1,300,000 Canadians who are out of work because of this government's deliberate economic policies, this is the blackest day in history; not some distant period. It is today.
My question is for the Minister of Finance. Today, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs reported that this January alone, 5,991 more Canadians went bankrupt, an increase of 69 per cent over the same period last year.
When speaking of these numbers, the Superintendent of Bankruptcy said: "You have to look at the emotional toll it is having. There are some really tragic stories".
Why does the minister have an economic plan that is forcing these thousands of Canadians into bankruptcy? Why does he pursue policies that are creating these tragedies all across this country? Why will he not make a commitment today to end these tragedies and get us out of this recession without further delay? Why will he not do that?

Mr. Speaker, I ask my hon. friend to look at not just the numbers which are a tragedy. I agree with him on that. However, the point the hon. member misses is that the percentage of bankruptcies in relation to the size of the economy, the number of businesses in the economy, today is .8 per cent. Back when he was on this side of the House in 1982, it was 1.28 per cent.
I am not saying that the picture we have today is a good picture, but I ask him to put things in perspective and to look in the mirror himself at the mess he was responsible for back in 1981-1982.

Mr. Speaker, this minister has been in his place for the past six years and he has to take responsibility for his mess and answer for that mess.
My supplementary question is also for the Minister of Finance and is about his policies. Last week, the Minister of National Revenue admitted what Canadians have suspected all along, and that is that this government is looking forward to having a multi-billion dollar revenue windfall from its infamous GST.
Why did the minister tell Canadians that the GST would be revenue neutral, when the Minister of National Revenue has admitted that it would bring about a multi-billion dollar tax grab for the government?
Was the government misleading Canadians about this, or is it simply saying that it does not know what it is doing? Which is it? I ask the minister to tell us which is it. Canadians want to know the truth.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I repeated what we had been saying all along, and that is that we do not expect any additional revenue from the GST at this time and that all factors have in fact been taken into account.
I did go on to say, upon questioning, what both the Minister of Finance and others have said in the past, that in the future if circumstances change, if we come out of the recession and so on, that there is a possibility of additional revenues taking place.
If the hon. member is interested in the facts, he will listen to this. I concluded by saying: "In any event, as we sit here now, we are talking about a hypothetical situation because we do not know for sure at this point in time if there is going to be excess revenue or not".
Mr. Speaker, may I first take this opportunity to express on behalf of my party best wishes for a very speedy recovery by the Leader of the Opposition.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister will be well aware of my party's views on the gulf war. We opposed its start because we felt that economic sanctions and diplomacy should have a chance to work. We oppose its continued escalation because we believe that what will result is certainly more
February 25, 1991

martyrdom to support Saddam Hussein. We want to see Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait as much as anyone does.
What we see is what President Bush is prepared to do and what action he is prepared to take. I want to ask the Prime Minister what his views are on behalf of Canada in terms of what the Canadian government's objectives are in this war. Will the Prime Minister ensure and demand at the United Nations that the United Nations make an assessment of when the mandate of the resolution has been adequately fulfilled and not simply allow the United States to make that judgment?

Mr. Speaker, I of course join the distinguished House leader of the Official Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party in conveying our veiy best wishes to the hon. member for Beausejour. We look forward to welcoming him back to the floor of the House of Commons in good health at a very early moment.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party asks what the objectives of the government are in regard to the prosecution of the war. They are the fulfilment of the resolutions of the UN Security Council. That is precisely what the government has done, precisely what the 30-odd members of the coalition are in the process of doing.
My hon. friend says that the NDP wants to see Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait as much as anyone. Well, you do not do it by wishing; you do it by taking action to defend principles.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister.
It is not very useful to the young Canadian men and women and others who are in the Middle East, and indeed to those hundreds of thousands of people in the Middle East who are suffering and are innocent victims of this war, to talk now about whose principles should reign.
The Prime Minister and I have different views about what would have ended Saddam Hussein's aggression. However, I am sure there is one thing we can agree on, and that is that we all wish our troops home safely.
Oral Questions
We know what the Prime Minister is doing to participate in the escalation of the war. What is he and his government doing to participate in bringing about a quick end to this war and about proposing peace proposals that will work or supporting other diplomatic initiatives that will bring this war to an end? I would like to ask the Prime Minister specifically what he himself has been doing to initiate or support other diplomatic initiatives to bring this war to an end?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend says that she knows what could have ended Saddam Hussein's aggression. So do we all. Saddam Hussein could have said and should have said: "I have taken illegal action against a neighbouring state. I am going to withdraw pursuant to the demands of the United Nations Security Council". When he refused to do that, it was no longer appropriate to accept the view that we will do nothing. Canada chose to join with the nations of the world and do something to liberate Kuwait and to drive him out of that country.
My hon. friend asks whether Canada has been playing an active role in regard to post-war hostilities toward the ending of the conflict. I think it is probably fair to say, and perhaps on behalf of all members of the House, it is widely known that the Secretary of State for External Affairs of Canada has been playing a leading role here, in Europe and elsewhere around the world in looking for effective means that would bring this war to an end. On behalf of all members of the House, I congratulate him on his tireless efforts to bring about a peaceful solution to the war.
Hear, hear.

It is widely known what could end the war. There are various opportunities now for a productive post-hostilities peace and reconstruction. In all these efforts Canada has played and will continue to play what we hope and believe is a helpful and constructive role.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
I regret that the Prime Minister could not give us specific details. If indeed the minister responsible for

February 25, 1991
Oral Questions
external affairs is making these diplomatic initiatives, surely it would be in Canadians' interests and Canadians would be interested in knowing exactly what they were.
I have another matter.

-the Prime Minister said yesterday that Canada may increase its participation in the gulf war. Right now, that particular region needs humanitarian aid for refugees, for innocent people who are homeless and without food.
On February 5, the Secretary of State for External Affairs told me in a letter that the government was prepared to increase its financial contribution for humanitarian aid if the need arose. Obviously, the need has arisen. Instead of increasing our participation in the war effort, why doesn't the government act on commitments made by the Secretary of State and increase humanitarian aid?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I answered a question from a reporter who said-

"Prime Minister, do you see at any point in this ground war that we might commit further resources to the war? Answer: We may have to, yes. In what capacity? I do not know". You asked me a hypothetical question. It is possible, but I cannot tell you in what area. It could be in one of a number of areas, I suspect.
The government responds to requests from our leading military advisors. All this indicated was that should a further request come forward, we would consider it and respond, as we have from the very beginning.

The hon. member inquired about the contributions mentioned by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The fact is that for the past few weeks, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has appeared two or three times a week before the House committee. He has given very specific details on his own and the Canadian government's initiatives in a variety of areas, including the search for a peaceful settlement of this conflict. He was elaborated on the various types of initiatives the Canadian government has taken and intends to take with respect to humanitarian aid. He described how the Canadian government intends to play a peace-keeping
role, if asked to do so, following the current military intervention in the gulf. He also mentioned that with a contribution of over $75 million, Canada was, on a per capita basis, one of the biggest donors in the western world with respect to humanitarian aid in the region.

Mr. Speaker, I too have some questions for the Prime Minister.
Speaking after the war cabinet yesterday, the Prime Minister made statements that appeared to go substantially beyond the mandate of the UN set out in the resolutions as passed by that body. The Prime Minister spoke of dozens of reasons why sanctions should be maintained against Iraq after the war is over and it has been expelled from Kuwait.
I wonder if the Prime Minister could tell us what are these dozens of reasons why he believes that economic sanctions should be enforced after the war is over and after the expulsion takes place.
Is it purely to force an arms embargo, or are there other objectives that the Prime Minister is now setting for the conduct of the war that have not yet been spelled out yet to the Canadian people?
Is the Prime Minister setting a new set of war aims of this case? In fact, are the statements yesterday not really contradicting in a very fundamental way the spirit set out in the speech he made three weeks ago announcing a peace plan for the Middle East?

Mr. Speaker, the version of my comments yesterday given by the member would lead to that conclusion, yes, but the statements he attributes to me are not borne out by any analysis of the transcript.
The question was: "What about the possibility of economic sanctions continuing once the war is over? Is that possible? And if they were to continue, why would that be done? Answer: I think that would be for the UN Security Council to consider. I can think, quite frankly, of a dozen different reasons why it might be helpful that they be maintained in total or in part for a period of time".
One of the reasons that I gave-if my hon. friend wishes, I can give others-would be that the Security
February 25, 1991

Council would surely decide that it would be imprudent, given the destruction of Kuwait, which is ongoing as we speak, the attempted invasion in respect of Saudi Arabia, and the Scud missiles launched against Israel, a noncombatant member in that region, to permit Saddam Hussein after hostilities ceased to rebuild a military machine that would give him access to the same kind of violence against innocent states such as Israel and Saudi Arabia.
It was in this light that I would invite the Security Council, after hostilities, to review the situation and to proceed with the greatest of prudence to make sure that these kinds of Scud missile attacks are never launched against Israel or any other country in the region.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a supplementary question.
Relating back to the United Nations, on the weekend the Secretary-General made the statement that the UN resolutions against Iraq could be upheld while still addressing the moral imperative of preventing further destruction.
We know this appeal of the Secretary-General was not successful this past weekend, but can the Prime Minister tell us if there are efforts now under way to maintain and continue the role of the United Nations in determining the outcome of the war?
Specifically, with respect to the answer he just gave, is the Prime Minister now saying that Canada is going to take the Security Council proposals for new resolutions that would extend sanctions after the war?
In other words, is Canada now taking the initiative to broaden or to change the objectives? In fact, what is the role of the Security Council going to be in the management of the war and, in particular, in trying to manage the peace itself? Can he explain what the Canadian position and role will be in light of the answer he just gave?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is one thing for the member for Winnipeg South Centre to take liberties with statements that the Prime Minister makes or that I make.
Oral Questions
I think it would serve the interests of us all if he did not take liberties with the statements of the Secretary-General. If he recalls, I had to call him to order on it in committee.
This is not the first time that he has taken one phrase from a statement by the Secretary-General and then attributed to the Secretary-General a meaning quite different from what the Secretary-General of the United Nations had indicated.
That is not a very helpful process for anyone who is interested in conducting an honest foreign policy in this country or indeed in his party.
Order.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think one of his colleagues has had enough.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
This past weekend and indeed yesterday, the Prime Minister indicated that further Canadian troops and equipment might be sent to the gulf. This morning on television the Minister of National Defence indicated that those might be further CF-18s.
I want to ask the Prime Minister if any decision has been taken or if any decision is contemplated to send further Canadian personnel and equipment to the gulf and what they might be.

I think the answer, Mr. Speaker, is one that I gave in response to a question from his colleague.
The transcript is very clear. It indicates that the question was: "Do you see at any point in this ground war that we might commit further resources?" The answer was: "We may have to, yes". That is depending on the recommendations that we receive from General de Chastelain and his colleagues of the senior military.
We have not yet received such requests but, if we do, we will consider them very carefully and respond in the national interest.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of National Defence.
Last month, the minister was quoted as saying that military costs could rise fourfold if the war continued to escalate. Now that the war has escalated, what is his

February 25, 1991
Oral Questions
estimation of our cost to the war effort at this time including any contemplated personnel or equipment we might send in the future?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the quotation to which the hon. member refers was in the very context of the question he has asked. Someone asked a hypothetical question and I said I was not going to get into something that would say it was forefold because I do not have that knowledge. For the same reason, I cannot answer the hypothetical part of his question.
It sounds like a lot of buffalo to me.
The member for Winnipeg South Centre is talking. I cannot hear what the hon. member is saying now.
The cost.

The cost, as I have enunciated, is approximately $60 million a month in incremental costs. There is $30 million associated with ongoing costs.
The hon. member would be aware, I know, that the more hours, the more duty, the more time which are placed upon the CF-18s in fulfilling their missions, there will be additional costs. We have not been involved in the additional role of air-to-ground for a long enough period of time to estimate what that additional costs may be.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Unemployment, I say to the minister, is way up. There are thousands more Canadians who are having to go on to welfare. We just learned that bankruptcies have jumped by 69 per cent from last year.
All of us have seen these human tragedies in our communities during this break, men and women whose lives quite literally have been tom apart by this recession.
Is the minister prepared to tell us today that he is going to change direction in his budget tomorrow, stop
listening just to big business groups and start to put these people who are being so badly hurt first in his considerations.

Mr. Speaker, I think there are two things that the hon. member neglected to mention. One is that we have been responding to the weakness in the economy by bringing down interest rates. They have come down by over 400 basis points, 4 percentage points since the peak last spring.
In addition, I should point out to the hon. member there has been a substantial net increase of businesses in this country even during this year of recession. There is a net increase of 130,000 businesses and that means there are a good deal more new businesses being created.
As I said in response to a previous question, one commentator from the Faculty of Management, University of Toronto says 160,000 new businesses have been created. Those are incorporated businesses. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business says that the figure is over 300,000 so there is a good deal of additional potential employment being created by these new businesses.
We on this side of the House want to bring down interest rates to ensure that those new businesses are given a lease on life so that they can create new jobs, new opportunities and grow to the benefit of the whole country.

In fact, Mr. Speaker, 327,000 Canadians lost their jobs last year not according to the Minister of Finance, but according to Statistics Canada. Three hundred and twenty-seven thousand Canadians lost their jobs permanently.

A Tory spokesman, the hon. member for Halton- Peel, said in referring to the Budget:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There have been some discussions and the Chair feels it is appropriate that our friend and colleague, the Hon. Eugene Forsey, receive the proper comments from this House. I would call to begin the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier.

subtopic: THE LATE DR. EUGENE ALFRED FORSEY
THE LATE DR. EUGENE ALFRED FORSEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians, particularly this House and this Parliament, suffered a loss last week with the passing of Dr. Eugene Forsey.
Dr. Forsey would never have been one to make this claim, since we knew him to be a man who never saw himself in terms of importance. He was a great Canadian.
I got to know Dr. Forsey during the years I spent in Parliament. Many a time, he gave me advice, a good argument, and many a time, some very good consultations.
Only a few weeks ago in a television interview, he said that he himself had never really accomplished much, although he admitted that he may have had some effect on one or two individuals. In fact, over a life of more than 86 years, he had a profound effect on many individuals and in that he accomplished a great deal.
Bom in Newfoundland, raised in Ottawa, educated in Montreal and Oxford, all of this shone in his personality. He was a brilliant scholar, a remorseless critic, a com-

mitted social reformer, a staunch federalist and a great Canadian patriot.
His thoughts were always framed in terms of a broad philosophy, but he was always demanding and always a stickler for detail. He brought remarkable energy and a distinctive turn of phrase to every endeavour he touched.

Eugene Forsey, that eminent politician, was raised in a conservative environment, later became one of the founders of the CCF-a socialist party, the ancestor of the NDP-and even ran for that party, and then, like any intelligent creature, reserved the right to change his mind and finally became a Liberal senator, thus moving from right to left to centre.
Later in life, he was reluctant to support a particular political party, preferring to pursue his objectives with the same vigour he had shown in defending his ideas, eschewing any form of partisanship.

The most remarkable thing that Dr. Forsey accomplished was his lack of pretence. He spoke in the same tones to young students as to Prime Ministers, took the same pains in expressing his views to many of us. We disagreed sometimes, but most of the time we agreed that it came from a very respected Canadian.
His memoirs speak of his life on the fringe of great events. History will show that frequently he was a constructive influence in the centre of this country.
We will miss Dr. Eugene Forsey.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: THE LATE DR. EUGENE ALFRED FORSEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we had attempted only a week ago to say a few kind words about Dr. Forsey in the House of Commons, we would have expected within 24 hours to receive a letter from him correcting our grammar, correcting our interpretation of history, or simply upbraiding us for having wasted the time of Parliament on something so unimportant as Eugene Forsey.
Sadly, none of us will receive such a letter from him now because last week, at the age of 86, Eugene Alfred Forsey died.
Tributes
Those of us who were privileged to work with him in this Parliament knew him as a scholar, as a statesman, as a passionate Canadian, and above all as a friend.
I first was privileged to meet Dr. Forsey over a decade ago when I served with him on the Joint Committee on the Constitution. He demonstrated both a formidable knowledge of Canada's Constitution and a fierce independence of mind and principle that caused him over the years to clash with the constitutional views of each one of Canada's political parties.
Knowing him in that capacity and as the distinguished co-chair of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, when he fought to protect the rights of Parliament and the rights of our ordinary citizens, I developed a deep regard for his intellect, for his courage, and for his passion for Canada.
We frequently did not find ourselves on the same side of issues, but opposing the views of people who felt privileged to know him as a friend was not an uncommon experience for a man who entitled his memoirs A Life on the Fringe. One might disagree with the policies he was proposing at any one time, but there was never any doubt whatsoever about his intellectual rigour, his courage, his love of Canada, or his willingness to fight fiercely for what he believed in.
We are fortunate that last year Eugene Forsey was finally persuaded to publish his memoirs, a witty, modest, and wonderfully readable account of his life and of Canada, from the time that he was bom in Grand Bank, Newfoundland, in 1904.
In the preface to his memoirs he explains why he resisted for so long the request that he publish his autobiography. In his words: "I replied that I'd sooner be sentenced to penal servitude. The thing wasn't worth doing; it would mean an appalling amount of work and I could not endure the thought of yet another editor determined to correct my English."
We can all be grateful that he was prevailed upon to commit to print his recollections of such a wonderful life.
We can be even more grateful for that life itself, which was dedicated to the service of this country. It is truly the case, as the Prime Minister said last week, that Canada

Tributes
has lost one of its most eminent sons with the passing of Eugene Forsey.

subtopic: THE LATE DR. EUGENE ALFRED FORSEY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: THE LATE DR. EUGENE ALFRED FORSEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to follow the member for Ottawa-Vanier and the Minister of Health and on behalf of the New Democratic Party to pay tribute to a great Canadian, Eugene Forsey.
In the past week, much has been written and spoken, all graciously and positively, about the late Eugene Forsey. I think the former senator would be surprised and I hope delighted considering what he said, and especially what he wrote in his long and illustrious career, about the same politicians, political parties and commentators.
The Globe and Mail said that he was the best read and best known constitutional expert. The Prime Minister has called him, as the Minister of Health has just pointed out, one of Canada's most eminent sons. I can imagine what the former senator's reply would be to that one, probably in a letter to The Globe and Mail.
I want to note Eugene Forsey's involvement with the labour movement. From 1942 to 1966, which is for some people a lifetime's contribution, for Eugene Forsey it was only part of a lifetime's contribution. In 1941, I am told he won a Guggenheim fellowship and he went to the United States to study.
In 1942, he came back and was offered a job at the Canadian Congress of Labour which in 1955 became the Canadian Labour Congress.
He was research director, and as such he wrote countless briefs. He spoke everywhere. He advocated issues, especially old age security, and was eminently successful there. He did it in English and French.
Claude Jodoin the distinguished first President of the Canadian Labour Congress used to compliment Dr. Forsey on what Monsieur Jodoin called his "beautiful French".
Dr. Forsey's intellectual labour, his precision and crispness helped build organized labour in Canada. I believe we and the country have all benefited from that.
He ran unsuccessfully, I guess I have to point out, as CCF candidate in two federal elections and in one provincial election; the provincial election against George Drew, the premier of Ontario.
If I might say on a personal note, he told me just a few weeks ago of that debacle and that election. Also, he told me about his associations with the likes of Stephen Leacock, Frank Scott, Norman Bethune, not to mention Mr. King, as he would call him, Arthur Meighen or John Diefenbaker.
To my generation of parliamentarians, he made history come alive. We sometimes met him for dinner at the Parliamentary Restaurant on a cold winter night. You could go there, and there was Eugene Forsey. He would talk to you, not patronizingly but wisely and intellectually about the great personages of Canadian history and the great issues. If we did not like that, we would discuss Meech Lake for dessert.
He was lucid right up to his death. Many people were surprised to see in last weekend's paper his criticism of the Allaire report, a more critical and analytical work than was done by any Canadian politician or journalist. That is an amazing tribute, and for this we will miss him a great deal, especially now. All members of the House know what I am speaking about.
I think our best tribute, as parliamentarians, would be to live up to his standard. He was precise, committed and visionaiy. He did it with wit and respect for those who did not share his views. I can see that smile now. I see the twinkle in his eyes and think of his recitation of all the figures in Canadian history.
He was not a man of malice. He was not an idealogue, but he was a man of principle. Yes, he was a bit of a maverick. He joined three political parties of this House of Commons and he quit them, too. This is probably a lesson that you can achieve a lot outside the political system as well. He had a consistent view, a consistent vision of Canada which some people disagreed with and others happened to agree with very much. However, whatever you felt on his positions you knew it was done with vigour, wit, intelligence, precision and it was well held in principle.
Canada is going to miss him. You cannot replace people like this.

That, notwithstanding any Standing Order or Special Order of this House, at 4.30 o'clock p.m. on Tbesday, February 26, 1991, the Speaker shall interrupt any proceedings then before the House, and such proceedings shall be deemed forthwith adjourned, and the House shall proceed forthwith to the consideration of the following motion, to stand in the name of the Minister of Finance, for the purpose of the budget statement of the Minister of Finance.
"That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government"-;

That, the resumed budget debate be in accordance with the Standing Orders.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the Standing Orders there are long-standing provisions going back decades, Standing Orders 84 and 83(2), that provide for the establishment of an Order of Day for the hearing of the budget simply by the minister standing in its place, but that was a time when we sat in the evenings and the budget was usually done at eight o'clock in the evening after the markets had closed.
Now those provisions do not allow us to start a budget at the usual time. Government Orders commence while the markets are still open in this country and it is inappropriate to give a budget at that time, so that is the reason for this special motion which is necessary as a result of the Standing Orders not keeping up to the change we have made in the hours of sitting in the House.
Last week when the government indicated that it was prepared to present a budget in the House on Tuesday, February 26,1 and my colleagues contacted the opposition parties and Independent members as well, to review the schedule the government had proposed and, generally speaking, there was concurrence with that. So, today, we hoped to finalize the timing of the budget presentation by asking that the House concur in this motion and we can then proceed with other business.
I understand that some members have expressed a desire to speak to this proposed motion. I understand that desire and I understand that after a limited amount of debate there will be a disposition to pass the motion and move on to other orders. That is a brief explanation of why the motion is here. We have had considerable discussions and I would hope that we would be able to proceed with this motion relatively soon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the opposition quite naturally will agree to this proposed order regarding the presentation of a budget, I think it important to take a few minutes to put a number of things on the record.
This is the first time that I have been called upon as opposition House leader to co-operate with the government in arranging the business of the House. I want to make it perfectly clear that I hope I shall be in a position to provide this kind of co-operation on most occasions.
It should be noted, however, that co-operation is very much a two-way street. It is my intention to approach discussions about House business as my predecessors have done in a reasonable and understanding manner, and I expect that the leader of the government in the House will do the same.
While the underlying assumption in parliamentary democracy is that the majority shall in the end prevail, it is essential as a facet of the process that the minority has the right to express its views in full. This House represents all of the people of the country, including the 57 per cent who did not vote for the government in the last federal election.
While we accept the parliamentary results of our democratic system and the legitimate expectation of the government that its proposals will be brought to timely decisions, we also insist on exercising the rights that the same system grants to us.
We know that you have a responsibility to ensure that our rights as a minority are maintained. We hope, however, that the government will be able to proceed with the normal courtesies-I underline those words
February 25, 1991

-that will lead to these rights being respected as a matter of normalcy.
It is well known that the government has initiated a discussion with the other parties in the House concerning the rules and procedures of our proceedings.
We enter these discussions with every expectation that the result will maintain the balance between the legislative needs of a duly elected government and the Canadian people's demand for thorough and proper examination in Parliament not only of the government's proposals, but also of all of its actions.
This is best accomplished through the normal co-operative conduct of the business of this House through honest and meaningful consultation. Our agreeing today to this order is an example-and I want to underline it for the government House leader-of our willingness to make this system work.
I want to get his assurance that in the future with all matters pertaining not only to government business, but indeed to all activities in this House, he will respond with courtesy, with meaningful consultations and not with a whip.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to spend just a couple of minutes on this motion.
I do so not from the perspective of the House leader of the Liberal Party. It does not seem to me to be useful to have a great deal of debate or discussion about co-operation at this stage. We certainly feel that this is a sensible motion. There is no problem with our reaction to it.
However, in a sense it is a motion which sets out the procedure for the budget. I want to say that from my perspective as the critic in my party responsible for responding to the budget and making suggestions with respect to the budget and so forth, it is unfortunate that the budget is being presented in this House with so little lead time before it in terms of House business.
We would certainly ourselves have appreciated the possibility to make use of some opposition days to put forward some of our suggestions with respect to this budget. For instance, the Minister of Finance today suggested that our position as a party was that we simply wanted to see a great deal more spending take place in
Government Orders
this country. We wanted to see the deficit expand, et cetera.
It would have been very useful to have had the chance for some preliminary discussion so that we could point out to the minister that that is certainly not our position.
Our position is very clear. It is a position which says that there is a massive interest rate gap between ourselves and the United States, something which historically is usually a gap of about 1 to 1.5 percentage points. It has become a gap of about 4 to 4.5 percentage points. In fact, this gap has been consistent for virtually two years now.
As a consequence of that massive gap between the two interest levels in our two countries, the Canadian dollar is at a level which frankly makes many of the businesses in my community and many of the businesses in communities across this country uncompetitive. Despite the fact that the skilled workers are there, that good investment has taken place, there has been a sabotaging of the efforts of many of these companies because of the high value of the dollar which has reflected the high value of interest rates in this country, not in an absolute sense, but relative to interest rates in the United States. Therefore, we have stressed the need to reduce that gap so that it returns to its historical level.
The interesting thing is if that is done, we would save as a country in the first year at least $5 billion in interest payments on our national debt because we would be dealing with lower interest rates.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (for Mr. Milliken) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-91 be amended in clause 6 by striking out line 19 at
page 4 and substituting the following therefor:
"the service or the use of the facility to the user or classes of user who benefit thereby."
Motion No. 2.
That Bill C-91 be amended in clause 6 by striking out line 47 at
page 4 and substituting the following therefor:
"lation or order provided that such rules for adjustment may not provide for the consideration of any new factors for adjustment of the amount of a fee or charge."
Motion No. 3
That Bill C-91 be amended by deleting clause 6.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the consent of my colleagues to speak on this issue.
First of all, let me say that the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, who proposed our party's three amendments, has done an excellent service on behalf of many people who have come to him, to me as well as to our party, to discuss the potential implications of these amendments to the Financial Administration Act.
In brief, we applaud the government for many of the proposals which it has put forward in this bill. We feel that many of the housekeeping amendments which it has made have been long overdue. Many have been recommended by the Auditor General for a number of years.
We commend the government for dealing with these important issues which are going to streamline many of the government operations. But it is wrong to assume that the entirety of this bill to amend the Financial
Administration Act deals simply with housekeeping amendments.
There are some provisions which give our party, the people on this side of the House, and many Canadians a great deal of concern.
The one that has caused the most concern is the one which deals with the concept of user fees. By these amendments the government is enlarging its power to impose fees or charges for services for any of the functions which it performs on behalf of Canadians.
You might ask, whether it is proper for Canadians who benefit to have to pay the cost. We do not do that in everything. We have a general revenue fund out of which we pay the costs of health, the costs of education; after all, it is not just students who pay the costs of education because we all benefit from having a highly educated populace.
The concept of user fees and charges can be taken to an extreme whereby one could destroy the basis of what this country is about, and destroy the basis for imposing taxes. If the concept is taken too far, only the people who benefit in any measure or used any type of facility would be the ones who would have to pay for it.
Let us be fair. There was not a groundswell of Canadians who came forward to speak to the committee about the problems created for their particular groups or industries because of this bill. But those who did come forward raised some very important concerns for us.
One of the major concerns was: How far is the government going to go in imposing user fees or charges? What are the real intentions of the government?
We asked this at committee and they said: "Well, we might have to charge a little more for passports to make sure that the costs of issuing passports are borne by the people who receive them. We may have to charge Xerox costs or reprinting costs."
We have no objection to small things like this, but they would not confirm for us that they were going to limit the powers granted to the Governor General in Council-not the subject of a debate in Parliament, but simply an Order in Council proposed by the government and written up behind closed doors.

We asked questions such as this: What is the government's hidden agenda? How far are they going to go? Will there be user fees for the Trans-Canada Highway? What about services at our airports? What about customs services for our importers and for our exporters? Should only they bear these costs?
What about the airport user fees themselves? Must they all be self-supporting and self-sustaining? It is taking the concept of privatization and pay-as-you-go to the maximum limit.
We have one particular industry which raised concerns with us, namely the shipping industry in Canada. Let us look at a bit of the background. A short while ago Transport Canada proposed that the shipping industry pay a higher cost for certain services rendered by the Government of Canada to it. However, it said that these costs were not going to be borne by pleasure craft owners or fishermen, but were going to be borne by our commercial shipping industry. These charges, according to the government, are going to be borne by the big shippers, those who ship grain, coal, iron ore and steel.
Who should pay for the costs of shipping services such as navigational services, search and rescue, ice-breaking, the Coast Guard fleet and navigational aids? Reasonable people are going to debate and have differences of opinion on who should bear the costs of maintaining a high standard of navigational safety and sophistication in Canada. We want the search and rescue operations of the Coast Guard, but who is going to pay for them? Should it be all boaters? Should part of it be out of the general revenue fund of Canada? These are issues which are critical to all of us as Canadians and must be the subject of debate and representations in the House of Commons.
For example, now the big shippers themselves pay for 100 per cent of Ports Canada. They pay for 100 per cent of the Seaway costs, the pilotage costs and most of the costs of the Grain Commission in Canada. But if we are going to extend the costs to these big shippers of these other services that Transport Canada is talking about, why will the government not come forward and say so?
What the government have said to us is that it does not know what it is going to do and it will not give us any
Government Orders
commitments as to how far it will go. Then it proposes some amendments to its own bill in response to these representations which have been made to it. I appreciate that the government is attempting to be forthcoming, but I really do not think the government heard or understood exactly what those representations involved.
First of all, what we as Liberals, and what the Milliken amendment attempted to do was to say that if additional fees are to be imposed on users as opposed to the general revenue fund or the budgets of departments, please make sure that it is borne by all of the persons who use that facility. In other words, do not just hit either the big persons or the small ones, or the foreigners who come into Canada, or the domestic people, or the people from central Canada; make sure that the users who benefit from those facilities are the ones who are paying for it. If you do not benefit why should you have to pay for it?
Should not the question of increased services to our shipping industry be the subject of open discussion with them? If they do not want those services why should they have to pay for them? Why should those services not be the subject of a political decision? Then the fees could come out of general revenue or departmental budgets.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands who has just come in here now, had proposed three amendments on our behalf. These amendments were designed to ensure that the persons who pay were the users who "benefited" from the services provided. Surely this is reasonable. Why would the government not have accommodated our party and the hon. member's proposal by allowing this simple amendment?
That is why, there is much good in this bill. We congratulate the new Treasury Board minister for his efforts in bringing forward this bill to update the law in the Financial Administration Act. But we do not want to give a blank cheque to the government, under the section 6 amendment dealing with user fees, to be able to impose the fees right across the board. It is arbitrary. It is against what we stand for in Parliament. It is unfair to those persons. It could hurt industries unfairly and that is why we have to oppose this bill, unless we can get the amendments which we seek.

speechtext:
I would like to address the motion made today by the hon. member opposite on Bill C-91. This is the aspect that has generated the most discussion, both in this Chamber as well as in committee. It is, of course, the amendment to section 19 in the act concerning user fees as proposed in clause 6 of this bill.
What section 19 of the Financial Administration Act is primarily concerned with is services that are provided to discrete and identifiable users or a group of users. The underlying principle is that, subject to program considerations, costs of services and rights and privileges should be paid by those individuals or groups of individuals.
I would be remiss if I did not underline the qualification in there: "subject to program considerations". The impact that fees will have on users, other affected parties and program objectives are very important considerations. In some cases there may be no user fees that should be imposed, or they could possibly be set to recover less than full cost, where imposing a fee or recovering full cost would jeopardize program objectives. On the other hand, not imposing appropriate user fees where circumstances warrant places an unfair burden on the general taxpayer.
An aspect of clause 6 that has been the subject of considerable discussion is the concept of setting fees by class of users. This change is intended to clarify that costs are to be averaged within classes when setting fees, where it is impractical to set individual fees every time a service is provided. While it may be decided for public policy or other program reasons that certain users should not bear the full cost of this service, it is not the intent that these costs will be recovered from other users.
However, concern has been raised that the current wording does not provide assurance that a class of users will not be charged more than the cost of service provided to that same class of user. In our view, taken as a whole, the current wording of clause 6 does provide this assurance. However, it may be useful to make it clearer.
The hon. member opposite proposes to do so through using the words, "to the user or classes of users who benefit thereby".
I do not want to take a lot of time, but I think we should indicate that this wording in itself has some problems. The phrase, "who benefit thereby" introduces a subjective test, whereas what is important is that a particular service or facility has been provided to a user or class of users.
For example, in the case of certain inspections falling under the Department of Agriculture, there is no question that a service has been provided, however one might argue who has been the ultimate person to benefit from that.
Accordingly, as an alternative to the wording suggested by the member opposite, I propose two amendments.
First, that motion No. 1 to amend clause 6 of Bill C-91 be amended by deleting all the words after the word "therefor" and substituting the following therefor:
"the service or the use of the facility to the users or class of users. ' '
Second, that motion No. 2 to amend clause 6 of Bill C-91 be amended by deleting all the words after the word "therefor" and substituting the following therefor:
"lation or order, but no such rules may provide for the consideration of any factors of adjustment that are not specified in the rules"
February 25, 1991

Government Orders
I think the House will see that this will in fact make the situation clearer for all.
