Mr. Speaker, it is a bit of deja vu for me to rise on this bill today. It takes me back to another bill in this House at another time, back in 1985. It was called the Canada Shipping Act, Bill C-75 and it was clause 4 at that time. That clause attempted through the front door to do what clause 6 in Bill C-91 is attempting to do through the back door and that is the imposition of user fees, particularly on the marine industry of Canada.
The government's attempt with Bill C-75 failed back then. This attempt must fail as well. If it does not fail it will be yet another nail in the coffin of Canada's maritime industry. In fact, it will go the way VIA Rail and other industries did in Canada at the hands of this government.
One more cost burden is being put on the marine industry that will only accelerate the following: the scrapping of existing ships owned by Canadian companies and turning them over to the wrecking yards; reflagging of the remaining salty-lakers on the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway; consolidation of steamship companies both on the Great Lakes and elsewhere. These actions in turn will see major job losses and major losses to the treasury of Canada and to the provinces and, obviously, increases to unemployment insurance and welfare.
I must say at the outset that the amendments put forward by the government do not deal with the real problem. While they are an attempt to make a bad bill slightly better, the problem still exists and that is the policy of this government and the implementation factor contained in this legislation that would allow them to proceed with the cost recovery measures.
As a nation that is based on exporting, we will at some point be without our own marine industry in which to transport our grain, coal, potash, as well as our other commodities.
In the short time available to me I want to quickly underline the procedural situation that we are in. We have the government that on the one hand is saying clause 6 of Bill C-91 does not in any way give it new powers as it applies to the marine industry. In fact, the Minister of Transport said in a letter on December 17, 1990, to the President of the Treasury Board:
It is my understanding that no new legislative authority is necessary to permit implementation of the department's proposals, should it be decided in due course to do so. In the opinion of the Department of Justice, the existing section 19 of the FAA (Financial Administration Act) provides a sufficient legal foundation.
The Financial Administration Act has been around since well before Bill C-75 was tabled in this House and debated. The question I ask and representatives of the marine industry ask is: if in 1985 amendments were needed to the Canada Shipping Act to allow for the Coast Guard's cost recovery measures to be implemented, why all of a sudden is no legislation required now?

Government Orders
Or if, on the other hand, the amendments in clause 6 are not aimed at the marine industry, who are they aimed at?
The marine industry has tracked this particular legislation from the time it came to realize that in fact it was a threat to it, that it would enable the government to do through legislative means what the industry believes, and certainly reports from the joint committee on scrutiny of regulations indicate, that the government under the old clause 19 does not have the power to implement a user fee or cost recovery mandate on the marine industry. In particular, the documentation provided by the Maritime Chamber of Commerce suggests that unless the fee is applied to a specific user, whether it is an individual or a corporation, at the request of that user or corporation, then legally the government cannot use the Financial Administration Act to levy cost recovery measures on the marine industry.
Throughout the debate at report stage and third reading, whenever we get to that, my colleagues and I will be outlining the impact of this legislation and the cost-recovery policy of this government, that is slowly working its way through the bureaucracy to the minister's desk, to indicate why it cannot go forward.
We have seen a major shift in transport where the marine industry has been declining because a variety of factors have pushed it into a weak position. For example, tonnages on the St. Lawrence Seaway have declined from 74 million tonnes in 1979 to 48 million tonnes in 1989, a drop of 35 per cent. Cargo volumes carried by the CSA fleet have dropped by 18 per cent from 94 million tonnes to 77 million tonnes during the same period.
The largest decreases have been in grain and iron ore where structural changes in the respective industries have been beyond the control of the marine industry. Government policy and shifting world markets are largely responsible for the drop in water-borne grain tonnage. The long decline in North American competitiveness in steel production has caused a major drop in the demand for iron ore.
Aside from a decline in markets, it should be noted that the inland marine mode itself faces heavy competitive pressures. Competition is being experienced from other modes, primarily rail, and other routings, Mississippi River, U.S. east coast, and Canadian west coast ports for grain only.
The result of forces at work on the marine mode is evident in the number of marine carriers which have had to sell, cease or consolidate operations in this increasingly uneconomic industry. The names of more than a dozen marine carriers have disappeared in recent times. In addition, existing marine carriers are consolidating bulk carrier operations as evidence of continuing pressure to reduce costs and provide for more efficient services.
In the past decade alone the number of actively trading ships in the CSA fleet has steadily declined from 176 in 1979 to 119 in 1989. According to the Canadian Lake Carriers' Association, the number of actively employed unionized seamen under their aegis has dropped from 3,592 in 1979 to 2,245 in 1990, a 38 per cent decrease.
This policy through this legislation will hit every region in this country. It will hit British Columbia in a very negative way. It will hit Ontario in a negative way. It will hit Quebec especially hard. It will also hit Atlantic Canada.
In doing so it will hit all of this country because without the ships to move grain, potash or coal from the prairies through the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway then the prairies will decline.
If we do not have ships moving then less steel is needed to build those ships. In fact, we have no ships being built; we have not had ships built for a number of years because of the policies of this government.
In spite of the last-minute tinkering by the government this particular aspect of the legislation is unacceptable. It is unacceptable to all of us who represent marine communities, who represent ports, who recognize the value of the marine industry in Canada. It cannot afford one more cent being added to its cost of operation.
What this government should be doing, instead of its cost-recovery measures, instead of this particular clause, is what the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority has been doing, developing lower incentive tolls to bring more products through the system so that more people can work, more people can benefit, and the country as a whole can benefit.

I urge the government to agree to entirely drop this particular clause, clause 6, amending section 19, so that the rest of the bill can go forward and this particular clause can be sent back to where it belongs and never seen again.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Before recognizing the next speaker I am in a position to say that, after taking under advisement the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls about the motion introduced by the hon. member for Cariboo-Chil-cotin and after due consideration, the Chair still believes that the two amendment motions presented by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance) are in order. Resuming debate. The hon. member for York West.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and speak at report stage of Bill C-91, which essentially encourages, through clause 6, the essence of cost recovery and generation of greater amounts of revenue for the federal government. Despite the amendments proposed by the parliamentary secretary, my party and this caucus have a great deal of concern with clause 6. We believe that clause 6 should be stricken from Bill C-91.
Clause 6 essentially says, on page 1990 of the bill, that the Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, (a) by regulation prescribe the fees or charges to be paid for a service or the use of a facility; and (b) authorize the appropriate minister to prescribe by order those fees or charges.
There have been a number of members who have alluded to the complications and the ramifications that this bill, particularly clause 6, would have on the shipping industry. The dramatic effects were in fact first discovered by representatives of the Great Lakes shipping industry.
In essence, it could mean an additional $25 million at the bare minimum in terms of additional charges being placed on a shipping and marine industry that, as has
Government Orders
been mentioned, is hurting. It is hurting in all regions of the country, particularly in the province of Quebec. Rather than trying to create a greater sense of confidence, rather than trying to create incentives, rather than trying to create policies that are going to be a shot in the arm to this particular industry, passing on greater cost recovery services to that industry is a way of aggravating an already bad situation.
Representatives from that industry are looking to this Parliament, are looking to this government, for reassuring signals that the government understands the plight of that industry, understands the importance of not trying to make it more uncompetitive, because they are already facing a very difficult competitive situation .The shipping industry is down anywhere from 8 to 12 per cent in various parts of the region, and therefore it can least afford at this time any additional costs on doing business.
It is not the first time that we rise in our places to try to come to grips with this problem. As the transport critic, on November 5, I raised this very issue when we were discussing the Port Wardens Act as it affects the ports of Montreal and Quebec City. We talked about the possibility that this is another way of trying to raise $25 million from the users, who traditionally have used the facilities provided by the federal Government of Canada.
We also raised on November 20, 1990, the possible ramifications of extended user fees to our various airline companies, particularly the smaller regional services in regions such as Atlantic Canada that will be hit the hardest. The scheme is not only unfair but it is unproportional, so that the smaller airlines based in Atlantic Canada, for instance, will in fact be paying greater amounts of cost recovery fees than the larger airline services in central Canada. As well, airports in northern Ontario will be paying more, proportionately speaking, than airports in Toronto, such as Pearson International, and other regional airports.
On November 2, I asked the very questions that we raise today, of the Minister of Transport, giving him and his administration yet another chance to try to come to grips with the problem.
Despite the many representations that have been made by colleagues on my side and by my colleagues in the New Democratic Party we have, as our first order of business, a piece of legislation that shows no sensitivity to the many representations made in this Chamber.

February 25, 1991
Government Orders
In addition, obviously the various interest groups have brought to bear their frustrations. Norman Hall, president of the Canadian Ship Owners' Association, in briefs and in submissions to the government, has made its position crystal clear on the ramifications that clause 6 would have on its industry. Mr. Peter Smith from the Chamber of the Maritime Commerce, in a lengthy and well outlined expose of the shipping industry, has also come to the same conclusion. Yet, as I mentioned moments ago, we are still trying to make the government understand the ailments of the shipping industry as one industry that would be impacted by the larger amount of user fees.
When we talk about user fees, we are talking about the greater movement, once again, to privatize. When we look at the transportation network in this country we have the privatization of Air Canada, we have the gutting of VIA Rail, we have the whole movement of deregulation that was supposed to be a Messiah for the country and for the travelling public and it has been the exact opposite. We have the privatization of Terminal 3 where the builder did his job. The builder designed a class operation in Terminal 3, but the jury is still out on what kind of job the government did because it is clouded in secrecy. Canadians do not know what deal was struck between the developer and the government.
So you cannot look at C-91 in isolation. Put together with the other aspects that have been part of the government's agenda it demonstrates a greater move to privatize, a greater move to deregulate and a greater move for the federal government, through Transport Canada, to divest itself, in one way or another, from its responsibilities and the infrastructure that has been created for many a year.
Our party will not stand idly by and watch the disintegration and removal of the federal government from this national infrastructure. While the world is changing before us, while the federal government needs to be flexible considering the political situation with regard to the Constitution; we also have to keep in mind the importance that transportation plays not only in terms of jobs, economic wealth and spin-offs, but also in what it means to the continuation of this country. It is a large country. We know that when we travel from our ridings. Some of us know it better, certainly than members from
Toronto, when we have to travel six and seven hours by plane. It is like going to Europe.
One of the forces, one of the networks, that has permitted this country to continue so successfully has been its transport infrastructure. I think, by the moves to VIA, by the moves to privatize Air Canada, by the moves to increase privatization, greater emphasis on user fees and greater pressure on the private firms which are having a tough time as it is, we are beginning to see the foundation begin to crumble.
I do not think we can see this bill in isolation because if we do we will-pardon the pun-miss the train, but it is in concert with the other moves of this government that we can see the big picture. The big picture is very troubling.
Therefore, I request our parliamentary secretary, who is the lead spokesperson for this bill on the government side, to rethink and to relook at clause 6. Our position would be to advocate a lifting of clause 6.
We had the minister, back in December, suggest to us that he was going to come back in February and give us his undertaking on what he is going to do with the whole question of user fees. We have yet to hear from the Minister of Transport. He has ushered no final position on the question of user fees. Therefore, let us not use the back door, as was mentioned already, to deal with an instance that should be dealt with clearly from a full, open perspective.
Therefore we are suggesting that this is an inappropriate way of dealing with a monumentally important issue.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing Bill C-91 and in particular the impact of clause 6 on our maritime industry and thus on our resource industries, I would just like to begin by saying that not only does this impose user fees on the transport marine industries, but it is also just another tax increase in addition to the 33 that have already been imposed by this government since its commencement.
One of the problems with the proposal before us is that it is open-ended. It is going to increase the costs of our maritime transport industry and thus our export cost for resources, just at a time when many of our exports

are in serious trouble as a result of many other aspects of this government's economic policies.
We have high energy costs, the costs of the high Canadian dollar, the memorandum of understanding on softwood lumber, and the grave difficulties that many of our coal shipments are having in the province of British Columbia. This latest thrust by the government, which is open-ended, will place us in an increasingly uncompetitive position with regard to these major resource exports.
Kootenay West-Revelstoke is an interior riding, a long way from the maritime industries some would say, but one thing has an effect on another. Within both the West Kootenay and the East Kootenay many of our mineral exports-from Cominco, for instance, lead and zinc, the largest smelter operation of its kind in the world, which is already undergoing a great many serious difficulties with regard to the effectiveness of its modernization program in which this government is a shareholder-are experiencing difficulties caused by this government's and the previous Liberal government's policies.
When it comes to the problems that the coal industry in the East Kootenay is having and the major difficulties that our softwood lumber industry is having all over Canada, but particularly in British Columbia where it is such a major part of our entire economy, more and more of our shipments of both exports and imports of these resource commodities are now being shipped through U.S. rather than Canadian ports due to both government inaction and bad government action.
We are afraid that the current proposal before us within this bill, and particularly with regard to clause 6, is going to complicate matters further at the worst possible time for those industries, the workers within them and the communities that rely upon them.
It is little more than a back door attempt to accomplish what clause 4 of Bill C-75 failed to do in 1985. Clearly it gives the government the legal ability to impose user fees on the marine industry and on our resource industries. If this attempt by the government does not fail, it will be yet another nail in the coffin of Canada's maritime industry and one more cost burden that will accelerate both the scrapping of existing ships and the consolidation of shipping companies which in turn will have very
Government Orders
deleterious effects. These actions in turn will result in major job losses, major tax losses and increased costs to both UIC and welfare as employees within these basic resource industries are impacted severely.
As our earlier speaker, the member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan, mentioned, I want to deal with the impact on certain specific commodity and industry groups. There is some ground for believing that the first-year target of $25 million envisaged by the government might well be conservative on the basis of the charges proposed. Information provided by shippers, port and industrial interests suggest that a limited number of companies and commodities, not more than about 20 in all, could pay upwards of $22 million to the cost recovery program.
More important than this total, however, are the potential sectorial shifts resulting from the additional transportation costs for market sensitive commodities in situations where the commodity, the carrier, or the port, is head to head with its competition. This is particularly true where the final delivered price is separated by a matter of cents from competitors who either do not pay the charge or enjoy a mileage advantage under the scheme.
While it is beyond our ability to analyse every movement, the Canadian Shipowners Association has identified certain commodities and situations which Transport Canada may have overlooked.
Marine traffic volumes of these selected commodities are, in the case of coal, some 30.8 million metric tons of exports to be effected and some 17.7 million metric tons of imports; in forest products, 18.6 million metric tons of exports and imports, simply .5 million metric tons.
In the sector of mining and metals, preliminary estimates suggest that as much as one-third of the total year one target of 25 million would be recovered as a result of movements of mineral and metal products. Shippers are particularly concerned about market share effects since transportation is a substantial component of the delivered cost of many raw materials. Thus, what may appear to be minor increases in the delivered costs of a number of commodities can cause sudden shifts in the delicate balance governing the ability to penetrate competitive hinterlands, resulting in lost sales and markets particularly to foreign competition free of this burden.

February 25, 1991
Government Orders
In the area of coal, most exports of coal are from west coast ports while imports and domestic movements are in the east. Imports include large quantities of U.S. coal used for electricity generation and steel production in southern and northern Ontario shipped from U.S. Lake Erie ports such as Toledo, Cleveland and Sandusky. Some western Canadian coal is shipped from Thunder Bay.
Very important from a cost sensitive point of view, however, is the movement of U.S. Appalachian coal currently moved from Cleveland by Canadian lakers for transhipment to very large bulk carriers at Sept lies proceeding to offshore markets. This move is particularly sensitive to transportation costs, since it is in direct competition with the port of Norfolk, Virginia, and will be jeopardized by the double imposition of the user charges.
Western Canadian producers of export coal are also highly concerned with the CCG cost recovery charges which they believe they will have to absorb. The large majority of these coal exports are metallurgical coals, the demand for which is flat or declining. The world market is highly competitive, and coal prices have dropped significantly.
Export coal producers located in British Columbia lost over $4.4 million in 1990. Export producers believe that their competitive position is already penalized by high Canadian rail diesel fuel taxes, high interest rates and an over-valued Canadian dollar, and that the new marine user charges will further impair their financial viability. This stresses what I was saying before, that this kind of action, open-ended as it is, comes at the worst possible time for the Canadian resource industry, particularly in western Canada.
Finally, in the matter of forest products, 39.8 million tonnes of forest products were transported by the marine mode in 1988. It has been estimated by the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association that the proposed cost recovery policy will cost the forest products industry approximately $4 million in additional marine shipping costs. Export shipments will absorb the majority of these additional costs.
In conclusion, additional transportation costs and declining traffic volumes could further disrupt transportation patterns and tonnages by upsetting the delicate competitive balance of key Canadian export commodities in U.S. and offshore markets.
The concerns of all these various interests must be rigorously addressed before any further steps are taken to implement the user charge scheme as currently proposed. That is why we take this position. We ask the government to rethink what it is doing before it drives one more nail in the coffin of Canada's resource export industries.

Mr. Speaker, this bill presently before the House should be called the collection agency's bill. The reason for that is because, of course, the clauses all complement one another-clauses 4, 5, 6, 7. What it does is bring a new element into fees and moneys owed to the federal government and that is the collection agency, those people who hound usually poor people for moneys owed to this or that person, this bank or this or that agency.
Under this legislation two entire sections deal with collection agencies. It even defines what a collection agency is, in case one cannot pay the fee imposed or one owes money to a federal government department. They define them as follows: a collection agency means a person other than an employee of a department-and department is defined in the Financial Administration Act as really being a department of the government- who (a) carries on the business of collecting debts for other persons and is registered or licensed as a member of the legal profession or as a collector of debts in the province in which the person carries on the business of collecting debts.
There are two things wrong with the legislation, and these are serious things. These are outrageous things to put in an act of Parliament. One is, of course, that you are going to charge all of these new fees and, second, you put into place a system of employing collection agencies to do all the collecting for you.
I suppose the signal to be taken from this is that the Government of Canada is saying the business to get into these days is the collection agency business. If you are not a receiver, then the collection agency business is the place to be according to this legislation.
There is something wrong with that. Suppose it is not your fault that you owe the money. Sometimes it is our fault that Canadians owe money; it is not their fault they owe money. This Parliament passed a law in 1988 called the advance child tax credit act or some sort of legislation. Right now in Canada there are debts owed to the Government of Canada by widows whose husbands perhaps died in November or December, or debts that

are owed to the Government of Canada because of a fire that took place in December and burned down a home and the children had to be put into a foster home for the month of January.
We passed a law that said that advance child tax credit payments would be paid out to mothers in the month of November in the amount of $518, I think it is, initially, and if you have no child care expenses you get an additional $38 or something like that, but you do not qualify for it unless every single child claimed was in your care in the past January.
Now we have the situation across Canada of single parents and widows owing money to the Government of Canada under this legislation. This authorizes collection agencies to collect that money, so there is a danger that sometimes it is not your fault that you owe the money.
The second thing that is unfair about these fees is that where they are in place in the fishing and shipping industries, for example, the fees favour foreign nations. I will give you one example, because I have a total of only 10 minutes as I understand it.
I was looking at some figures on the weekend of the Japanese take for blue fin tuna and sharks in Canadian waters. They do not have a quota, but they actually took 170 tonnes of blue fin tuna and 53 tonnes of shark without a licence and without a quota.
The way it is done legally is this. Of course, they caught it as a by-catch, more than Newfoundlanders or Nova Scotians are allowed to catch. They caught it as a by-catch. It was perfectly legal. They only caught their by-catch, and then they got out. They did not catch the other species they were fishing for.
They do not pay a fee for their licences. No foreign nation in the world pays a fee for their licences when they go to pick them up in the office in St. John's, Newfoundland or Halifax, Nova Scotia. A Canadian cannot get a licence unless he pays a fee.
What happens to all these fees? Over the years, they send bills to these countries. We see examples today of France negotiating half the fee that it owes for fishing off the east coast of Canada.
Government Orders
It is not fair to have Canadians bearing the brunt of these new fees and a different system, a discriminatory system, against our Canadian fishermen in place that lets all those foreign nations off the hook for all those fees that are supposed to be paid. Because they are all foreign nations, it is really done through the Department of External Affairs and billed over a period of years.
Mr. Speaker, you might say with the Japanese fishing fleets that they are the sharks and we have become the bait in the fishing industry.
There are many other things wrong with the legislation. I do not have time to go into it. I wish I did because if I did perhaps government members would vote against this bill.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in the debate this afternoon. The debate is rather interesting but somewhat old theme in this House since the arrival of the Conservative government in 1984.
What we are looking at today is yet another form of taxation on the people of Canada and the kinds of taxations that have occurred on the people of Canada. The public is absolutely outraged at this government. It is completely outraged.
It was expressed in an interesting way just early in the year when somebody pointed out that the present government is enjoying the confidence of about 12 per cent of Canadians. They suggested that to put that into perspective it was necessary to understand that 15 per cent still thought Elvis Presley was alive and that they had seen him in public more often than they had seen the Prime Minister.
Ultimately, the erosion of the confidence in this government is incredible. It is largely because of things like privatization, deregulation and cost recovery, the destruction of Canada's national infrastructure.
It is ironic that this government would have time after time taxed Canadians so heavily with not just income tax, but with charges such as these at every turnaround, driving up the cost of doing business in this country.
So often the cost of recovery comes out of the pockets least able to pay such as the goods and services tax, an enormously regressive tax. It is absolutely abhorrent to the vast majority of Canadians just as this proposal that affects the shipping industry will be today. The government forges ahead. The Prime Minister, at 12 per cent in

Government Orders
the polls, facing enormous opposition from every citizen in this country from coast to coast, except that stalwart 12 per cent, said: "Never mind, I know what is best for Canadians and I am going to do it no matter what they think about it".
In reality what has happened is that the Prime Minister neither knows what is best for Canadians nor enjoys any of the confidence in this country.
One of the things that is so catastrophic for Canadians is that this Prime Minister, in whom Canadians have no confidence whatsoever, is the person who is going to restructure Canada, who proposes new constitutional forums that are going to, by the look of it, decentralize this country, devolve Canadian federal government powers to the provinces and essentially Balkanize this nation. You have to ask why. Why the cost recovery, why the privatization, why the deregulation, why the devolving of powers to all the provinces and removing the strength of the federal government, the integrity of this nation?
One school of thought says that the trade agreement was not in fact a trade agreement, it was a proposal for economic union with the United States. The way that you would bring about an economic union with the United States is to not only negotiate the fundamental agreement, but also destroy the national infrastructure that holds this country together on an east-west basis. You would destroy the rail system, VIA Rail. You would sell off the national energy corporation that gives Canada a national energy policy from one end of this country to the other. You would sell that off, turn it back to one of the seven sisters or the equivalent.
You would in the process put in an open skies policy in which you allow American carriers to run the route from Vancouver to Toronto, and run it at a lower rate than Air Canada and Canadian could do it. You could destroy the national air transportation structure, completely destroy it, turn it over to American carriers, U.S. Air or American Airlines. That would destroy the east-west structure. The removal of the railroads, VIA Rail, would destroy the east-west structure that holds this country together.
You would then get rid of the communications system. You would begin by loading into the legislation something that destroyed the CBC, the national communications system that holds us together on an east-west basis.
Gradually, one step at a time, from 1984 through 1985, through 1986, through 1987, you would begin to undo this country, the infrastructure that holds the east-west nature of this country together against that enormous pressure from the south.
You would also put in things like foreign investment. You would remove any controls over foreign investment so that American firms could come into Canada and literally buy up Canadian firms. The Americans would not only be working with a destroyed infrastructure in this country, a destroyed national infrastructure, but they would also be dealing with a country whose economy was largely owned and controlled by foreign owners from the United States.
I have the greatest fear that one day the Prime Minister, in the not too distant future, still at 12 per cent in the polls, still behind those that believe Elvis Presley is alive, would come up and say: "Well, it is time to leave. I have achieved everything I set out to do".
It is interesting that the chairman of the finance committee, in a candid statement one day, said: "You give us two terms in here and nobody will ever put it together again". What an ominous statement for Canadians.
It would be interesting to know that down the road when this Prime Minister is not able to gamer any more than 12 per cent or 15 per cent in the polls and must leave, the Conservatives will put another leader in place. With the pig-headed determination to pursue such wrong-headed policies, policies that are completely opposed by Canadians, the only answer that he could give Canadians as he leaves office to be replaced by someone else that the Conservatives will use to try and get another victory would be that "I have achieved everything that I had set out to do". This is the systematic destruction of Canada: privatization, deregulation, cost recovery. Just a couple of quick, beautiful examples. Deregulation is an opportunity to let as many carriers get into an area and service an area as they possibly can and do it as cheaply as they possibly can. The Nanaimo-Vancouver run for aircraft is a beautiful example. They moved from two to five carriers. Had the
February 25, 1991

carriers pooled their money, built a bridge and put a toll on it, they would have made more money. It would have been cheaper for them in the long run.
When the five of them were involved the fare from Vancouver to Nanaimo was $17. The lowest fare that you could travel that distance was $17. Of course they went broke. Of course they had serious accidents, fatal accidents. Finally the two main carriers took over and now it is $96.50 to travel from Vancouver to Nanaimo, a completely outrageous monopolistic price.
I notice my time is running short. Let me give an example of cost recovery. The northern end of Vancouver Island, an area with a precarious economy, is working hard to build that economy and give a decent living to its inhabitants. National Revenue decided it was going to remove the customs office. What happens now is that in order to clear customs, to move in and out of that economy in the northern end of Vancouver Island, you must go somewhere else. If you go somewhere else and it is more expensive because of what the government has done in cost recovery, you might as well stay somewhere else. Gradually the economy on northern Vancouver Island begins to implode, to shrink and the homes and lives of people there are negatively affected.
They blame directly this government's wrong-headed cost recovery procedures, the same wrong-headed procedures that are in this bill before us today.
Hopefully it will withdraw the open skies policy. Hopefully it will withdraw this provision of the bill and begin to take some responsibility to provide a national infrastructure as a national responsibility so that local and regional economies can grow with that kind of sheltering and assistance.

Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to the attention of the House the effect of this legislation on communities in northern Canada, such as my own in Labrador. I am wondering if the House and the government have an appreciation of exactly what this will mean for northern communities. I am talking about resource based communities where there are no alternatives to the extraction of iron ore or to the catching of fish. I am talking about single industry towns which have
Government Orders
no alternative in terms of job creation for those people who live and who have lived there for 20 or 30 years.
When I talk about my own riding I could just as easily be talking about communities in northern Quebec, northern Ontario, northern British Columbia, the Yukon or the Northwest Territories. Those small isolated northern communities are resource based, have no alternatives and depend wholly and solely on those resource industries. They are also isolated for a great part of the year and depend on either sea transportation in the summertime to get goods in and to move goods out or depend on air transportation in the wintertime to do the same things for passengers and freight and commodities. Those are the communities that are going to be negatively affected by this legislation.
It is worth while noting that those communities, isolated, vulnerable, resource based with no alternatives already have imposed upon them airport user fees, whereby people travelling by air-there are no roads and there are no ships in the wintertime-must travel by aircraft, already have to pay on top of their high cost of transportation an airport fee. They will now have to pay GST on the cost of goods and services moved into those communities.
These communities already have the highest cost in Canada in terms of fuel. A litre of gasoline in my riding, for example, at this moment is close to $1. Does anybody else in Canada pay $1 a litre for gasoline? That is the kind of costs I am talking about. That is the kind of costs that companies and individuals have to pay that live in the north. Yet this government is now thinking about imposing a further cost.
We are not talking about handouts here. What we are talking about is the imposition of a further obstacle to survival on companies and individuals who live in northern Canada.
I am talking about the imposition of additional user fees on small airlines, for example. I am talking about the imposition of possible user fees on ice-breakers, where a long liner is caught in the ice in the springtime and an ice-breaker has to be sent in to set that boat free. That fisherman in that boat, who is already suffering

February 25, 1991
Government Orders
from a decline in the fish stocks off the Atlantic coast, could now be charged an additional user fee for freeing his boat from the ice.
What about search and rescue? Are we going to be charged now for search and rescue? If your life is on the line, if you are lost in a storm at sea, or if you are caught in the ice in the spring, would you have to pay a user fee now so that your life can be saved and your boat preserved?
This is the kind of cost that is going to drive companies and individuals in the north out of existence altogether.
I want to talk in particular about the iron ore industry. When I talk about the Iron Ore Company of Canada and Wabush Mines, I could just as easily be talking about mining companies in northern Quebec, northern Ontario, the Yukon, or the Northwest Territories, because all of those are going to have to depend on transportation to ship their product to market.
The Prime Minister will understand that because at one time he was president of the Iron Ore Company of Canada, president at a time when it was going through a great deal of difficulty. That company has gone through that troubled time. It has cut its costs, it has had some lay-offs, and it is now competitive in the marketplace. But it is not making a great deal of money; it is barely surviving.
If there is going to be an added imposition, an added financial burden on that company, it is going to drive that company that the Prime Minister formerly headed completely out of existence, as it will with other mining companies.
I want to read into the record what Mr. Muloin, the general manager of Wabush Mines, has to say about the legislation in question. This could very easily be any other mining community in the north. He says:
As you are aware, Transport Canada has resurrected the concept of user fees for the Marine Industry. This proposal will have a serious impact on the members of your riding.
Under the proposed legislation, international (including USA) customers will be charged $0.12 per ton for the iron ore shipped from the Canadian iron ore mines while Canadian customers will be charged $0.06 per ton.
This fee, if adopted, will increase the cost of Canadian iron ore products from the Quebec/Labrador area by over $4 million per year.
Iron ore is an internationally traded commodity that is currently in oversupply. It is therefore critical for producers such as Wabush Mines to remain cost competitive if we are to continue to sell our product and to remain in business.
This initiative by Transport Canada poses a serious threat to our ability to remain competitive and, as such, threatens the employment and living standards of the families that work in the Quebec/Labrador iron ore industry.
I urge you to convey our objections to this proposal to your colleague, the Honourable Doug Lewis, the Minister of Transport.
I have done that today, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister of Transport and to the Government of Canada.
I want to read into the record as well a letter from Mr. Bill Kelly, who is the Mayor of Wabush. And I am sure he is supported by the Mayor of Labrador City, and I suspect that he is supported by the Mayor of Fairmont and those communities over the Quebec border that also have iron ore mines as well.
Here is what he says:
We have been informed that Transport Canada is in the process of restructuring the concept of user fees for the Marine Industry.-
Wabush Mines has been able to survive and remain competitive in the iron ore business because they are very cost conscious and efficient. The slightest increase in cost per ton could mean the difference between a successful operation and one which is closed.
Wabush is a single industry town. Our existence depends on Wabush Mines being able to sell its product at competitive prices. To remain competitive and to reduce costs, Wabush Mines has reduced its workforce- We are very concerned that substantial increase in the cost per ton will result in more lay-offs or even a shutdown.
The Quebec/Labrador area produces 90 percent of the iron ore in Canada. This fee, if adopted, will increase the cost of iron ore produced in our area by over $4,000,000.00.
We are not talking about hand-outs here. What the government is doing is imposing a financial burden on those companies which will make it impossible for them to survive, to make sure that they do not maintain or create jobs, but in fact lay off people and close those industries in northern Canada.
We are not talking about financial support or handouts. We are talking about a fair chance to survive. This government, which supports the private sector and says quite rightly that the private sector is the only way to create long-term jobs, has to get its house and head in
February 25, 1991

order, and stop imposing fees on isolated, vulnerable, northern communities that are going to be driven out of existence if this government has its way.
That is why clause 6 of this legislation must be defeated.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to stand today and say a few brief words about the bill that is before us, Bill C-91.
I would like to preface my remarks by saying that in British Columbia where I come from, particularly the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt, the economy is based on agriculture as well as on forestry and to some extent on mining.
All of these things depend on the ability of the producers of these commodities to be able to ship their goods to the markets. Of course, being from British Columbia, the markets that we are looking at aside from the United States are the Pacific Rim markets.
Over the last number of years, we have seen major problems in the forest industry in particular, not only in British Columbia but throughout Canada.
In British Columbia of course, we have the free trade agreement, the Memorandum of Understanding between Canada and the United States that levied 15 per cent tariff on top of the price of the wood products that were being shipped into United States.
We have the artificially high Canadian dollar and artificially high interest rates. When the free trade debate was raging in 1987 and in 1988, the forest industry thought that perhaps as a result of this particular agreement they could have some benefit. It was contingent upon the dollar remaining low and interest rates remaining reasonable.
As history has shown us over the last couple of years, that has not happened. Interest rates have skyrocketed. The MOU came in. The forest industry has run into major problems, and this particular bill with the user pay feature in it for forest products is one more nail in the coffin.
In my province, this industry right now is in the throes of the recession and is having a hard time. As the recession goes world-wide, so goes the forest industry. If
Government Orders
they cannot sell their products to the housing industry, then they have a lot of problems.
More and more the problem we are seeing is government hitting this particular industry while it is down. The forest industry is more than a housing industry. It includes, of course, the major part of pulp and paper. The policies of this government have not helped in that particular instance. In fact, it has hurt one of our major producers in the province of British Columbia. By introducing cost recovery, we find more and more that this is what is happening to our industry and part of the reason why we are seeing major lay-offs in the province of British Columbia.
These lay-offs are having a major effect on access to unemployment insurance. Instead of taking two to three weeks to get their unemployment insurance benefits now these people are looking at six, eight, and sometimes 12 weeks in order to get those benefits. That, I believe, is a direct consequence of what this government's policies are, one more thing that is stuck in the way of increasing the ability of the forest industry as well as mining, whether it be in metallurgical mining, coal mining, or whatever, it is an extra cost that is being added. It is hitting regionally at areas like British Columbia, northern Ontario, and the maritimes.
These industries have to be assisted with those shipping costs to ensure that they are able to continue to produce and ship to export markets, to markets overseas, to ensure that we have increased industry, employment within our areas and the ability to add to the marketplace.
What I see in this also is some of the tendency of this government toward a major privatization. The user-fee aspect in itself perhaps is not that bad. But when you take it and add it to all of the other things of privatization, whether it be privatization of Petro-Canada, Air Canada, or whether the thrust will be toward the privatization of our rural post offices and the post office sector as a whole, it is a whole malaise that is going across the country through the actions of this government. This is simply one other plank, if you will, in the deck of privatization; it is privatization simply for the sake of privatization itself instead of a move toward something that will assist or help the people of Canada and the people of my riding.

Government Orders
One of the former speakers in this debate talked about the difficulty and the overflow in this area upon the air industry. I am sure that you know, the problems that the transportation industry has, especially with the addition of the goods and services tax, the actual triple taxation that the transport area is running into. They pay their taxation either at airports or at the marine facilities. They pay their taxation on their fuels. Now with the user fee they will be paying a fourth tax, aside from the goods and service tax added to the problem that they have got.
It seems that we are more and more getting to the area where we are pushing down those that in fact need some assistance. In Canada, with the long distances and transportation costs many of our industries need that assistance. Throughout the history of Canada we have always ensured that assistance was taken into consideration for the the development of mining coal, forestry, or whatever in a particular region.
We are seeing the abandonment of that principle in Canada. We are seeing the abandonment of the idea of Canada as a single united entity.
All of these things pick away at that particular part of the Canadian unity. When this government starts to realize and recognize the importance of all of this to the whole network, instead of compartmentalizing and beating down all of these individual sections, it may then have an idea of what we can do to unite this country.

Mr. Speaker, what we have been concerned about with respect to this bill is that the bill itself is an effort to increase the capacity of the International Monetary Fund to apply sanctions against less developed countries that run into problems with the IMF.

February 25, 1991
Government Orders
It is an interesting point which we can take up in the third reading debate whether it makes sense to move in this direction or not. But if we are to move in this direction of increased sanctions which the IMF is able to make use of vis-a-vis less developed countries, it seems to us in this party very important that there should be regular reports to the House of Commons from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. This would make it possible for the House to be aware of how these powers, in which we would acquiesce through this bill, are being used.
This amendment would include, within the proposed legislation itself, a commitment that whenever there was a meeting of the Interim Committee of the International Monetary Fund or the Development Committee of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the communiques emerging from those particular meetings would be laid before Parliament. That would make it possible for members of Parliament to be fully apprised of the way in which these new powers, which we are granting to the IMF, are being used.
I would just like to briefly explain the changes, for which I have asked for unanimous consent, which I have been given, from the House to put forward. It is not clear that within the usual scheduling of the IMF and the World Bank every six months is a figure which will be operative, that it may be five months on one occasion or seven months on another occasion until a meeting takes place of the Interim Committee and the Development Committee. That is the reason for taking out the every six months. The replacement of reports by communiques is simply to make it clearer that the documents which should be laid before the Parliament of Canada are the documents which emerge from the Interim Committee and from the Development Committee of the World Bank and the IMF.
As I say, I think it is important to establish the principle that these regular reporting procedures be established clearly in legislation. It then becomes the responsibility of the government to see to it that those reporting responsibilities are in fact met, and it becomes possible for members of Parliament to respond to those communiques when they reach the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the clarification because the citations in Beauchesne seem to imply that it would not be in order, so I presume we have established a precedent in this case.
I would first of all like to express minor concerns about the references in the amendment. When you review the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act and when you review the schedules to that act, the Bretton Woods agreements, it is difficult to understand in the context of the legislation itself what is the interim committee.
The interim committee exists and we are all aware of it, but as a legal or statutory entity I do not believe that it exists in Canadian law, either in the act or in the schedule. So I am concerned about the clarity of the drafting.
Furthermore, the reference to meetings of the interim committee, of the IMF and of the World Bank leave open some question as to what meetings in particular are being referred to.
Those being my concerns about the drafting of this provision, I would like to say that the substance of it, its intent to make the participation of the Government of Canada in activities of the International Monetary Fund in particular more accountable to the Parliament of Canada, is a very desirable objective. We have found over the years that in many ways the objectives, particu-

larly of Third World development, of realignment of Third World debt, have been frustrated by policies pursued by the IMF. Many times these policies are carried out without the direct knowledge of the Parliament of Canada.
To the extent that the amendment of the member for Essex-Windsor intends to present before the Parliament of Canada the substance of what is being discussed and debated and decided in meetings of the IMF and the World Bank, then I am fully in support of that.
I think that our party would like to see an increase in the accountability and the reports delivered by the minister so that we can be fully informed, so that the Canadian public and those in the media who report on matters of Third World development can be fully informed as to the status of our government's participation and of the decisions that are being made which in many ways are so important.

speechtext:
Somebody says there is little chance of that.
What I would like to say concerning Bill C-93 is that this bill provides us with an excellent opportunity to review some of the concerns that many of us have had about the International Monetary Fund and how it has impacted upon Third World development and problems.

February 25, 1991
Government Orders
That being said, it should be remembered that the issues raised by this piece of legislation reflect only two fairly minor amendments to the method by which the IMF functions. First of all, it increases the quotas which countries are obliged to hold on deposit with the IMF. Second, it introduces a new mechanism of discipline for those countries that are in default with the IMF, namely the suspension of voting privileges.
With respect to the first of these proposals, I think we find that there is general and perhaps entire support, with the possible exception of the United States, for increasing the quotas contributed to the International Monetary Fund.
These quotas which will not take effect unless they have been approved by an 85 per cent voting majority of member countries require that member nations increase their contribution to the fund.
In hearing this, I think all Canadians become a little concerned that this is yet another expenditure of government assets that is ultimately going to cost us all as taxpayers.
In supporting this bill, it is on the assurance by the government and by government officials that the method by which these quotas are achieved is the placing on deposit of assets with the IMF that then reflect the fact that these are assets of the Government of Canada.
In other words, we are assured that these increased quotas are not an expenditure item for the Government of Canada. They do not cost the taxpayer anything is what we are told.
Accepting that, I would note the concern that we have about the suspension of voting privileges for defaulting nations. It is true, as we said in the earlier debate on this-and I had the occasion to debate at that time this issue-that the IMF occasionally needs a workable method of seeking to enforce payment of obligations to it.
Until now that method has been the right to suspend member countries from participation in the fund, a somewhat draconian measure, one which has never been taken.
The suspension of voting privileges is much more usable as a disciplinary measure because the consequences are somewhat less grave. To do so, however,
essentially silences the voices of the countries that are weakest and that are most in need of the financial assistance provided by the fund.
To move in this way raises for many of us-I know for the member for Essex-Windsor as well-the concern that in using its impressive powers as a funder of international business transactions the IMF will further fail to hear in many cases the voices of those countries that are most in need of assistance.
We support this bill. I think the way to explain why, however, is best expressed in the words that were presented to us by Roy Culpeper of the North-South Institute when he appeared before the legislative committee on Bill C-93.
He referred to the concerns of many MPs about the response of the government to the report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade which was tabled somewhat earlier.
Although these concerns are there and although other organizations, including the North-South Institute, raised many concerns in appearing before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade as it completed its study, Mr. Culpeper advised us to go ahead with the bill. He stated:
I do not believe that Bill C-93 provides the best vehicle to carry forward this debate. In my view, Bill C-93 should be enacted so that Canada can give its support to help make the quota increase effective as early as possible. The IMF is not, to be sure, without its faults or without need of improvement. But this legislation does not provide adequate opportunity for a thorough and much-needed review of the IMF and for political input from our legislators and the public. The point I want to make is that Canada, probably along with most other member countries, lacks an adequate review process to ensure the accountability of this supremely important international institution to the public at large.
The point is that we have a bill which achieves certain objectives that the North-South Institute has endorsed but which fails to raise, in essence, the important issues of ongoing accountability of the IMF and concern for what is happening with respect to Third World development.
What we find is that many of the policies pursued by the IMF, well intentioned, structural adjustment policies, have not been terribly successful in improving the state of Third World countries. The result of IMF interference in the performance of some Third World countries, together with the increasing debt crisis in the
February 25, 1991

Third World, is that IMF policies have in some cases actually hurt the countries they were intended to help.
We typically had in the IMF medicine prescribed for ailing countries prescriptions for cuts in subsidies to the poor, devaluations, deregulation, and the intention of trying to create trade surpluses which had the effect of eliminating agricultural production that sustained the population and provided adequate food for them.
After nearly a decade of IMF adjustment, GNP per capita in the Third World, I am told, is 6 per cent lower than it was 10 years ago. Even on strict economic grounds IMF policies have often seemed to be unsuccessful.
We have these concerns. We have them in Canada and in other countries that have participated in support of the IMF. They are concerns that need to be brought forward, both in Canada and elsewhere, in debate as we approach, we hope, the imminent end of a war in the Persian Gulf. We concern ourselves with the frequent interpretation in Third World countries that this in fact is a war of the rich nations against the poor, that it is a war between the north and the south, interpretations that I do not agree with but which are there in these emerging countries. We have to face in that context what our population perceives as generous aid to Third World countries, with the realization that the flow of wealth continues to be not from north to south but the net transfer of wealth in the world today is from south to north.
While many of us, Canada and other countries, maintain a pretext of helping the developing countries of the Third World, the reality is that through our policies, through our debt structure, we continue to draw wealth away from Third World countries. We continue in many cases to draw their people away. We draw their best and their brightest through immigration policies that award points for skills and education. We find places in Canada for the very best of the Third World, but not for the very poorest or the very weakest.
In this context, I think all of us as Canadians have to realize that there surely will come a day of reckoning when the poverty, the hunger, the deprivation, the famine, the problems which exist that seem insurmount-
Govemment Orders
able in the southern hemisphere will come back to us for solution. If we do not begin to work on the basis of solutions today, the problems will be even more insurmountable tomorrow.
Therefore, as I said earlier, I support the amendment of the hon. member for Essex-Windsor that has been accepted in terms of its content. I hope that we will see increasingly the attention of parliamentarians in Canada and in other developed countries to the issues related to how we solve on a long-term basis the problems of the developing world. They are problems which we must recognize that we share as Canadians, and I suspect that members of the governing party are less likely to share this than some of us. But I think Canadians by and large do recognize that within Canada we must seek to find ways to ensure that all parts of the country share in some measure in the prosperity of our land.
It was one of the basic principles upon which Canada has expanded its Confederation over the years, one that we need to be talking more about today. Surely the same principle needs to apply on a global basis. Surely we need to begin to recognize that we cannot forever deny citizens of other countries a share in the wealth that we enjoy. It is not ours by right of any goodness that is inherent to ourselves. The responsibility lies on us as trustees of enormous wealth to ensure that poverty, disease and deprivation does not destroy the hope and the goodwill of people in whatever nation they happen to have been bom.
Therefore, we are looking at a technical bill in some ways, but a bill which has underlying it matters of great importance. It is important now that parliamentarians renew their efforts to address some of these issues.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was just starting to say before we decided to change course a little bit, this is a bill I would like to say just a very few things about.
First, this bill does accomplish an important purpose. It is one step in the agreement of the number of countries that will be necessary to increase the total financial resources of the International Monetary Fund to make it possible for that fund to lend more money to developing countries that are facing serious debt crises. We in this party support that goal very much.

February 25, 1991
Government Orders
Unfortunately, the bill also has within it, apparently under the influence especially of American representatives to the IMF, a number of increased sanctions which can be applied against developing countries if they find themselves in arrears to the IMF.
This becomes possible if this bill is accepted by this Parliament and, in turn, by a number of other Parliaments throughout the world. If that happens, it will be possible for the first time for the International Monetary Fund to actually suspend voting rights for member countries of the IMF.
Prior to this, it has been possible if the IMF becomes so concerned about a country which is in arrears to expel that country from the IMF, a solution which is so Draconian that it has generally not been adopted by the IMF.
This particular piece of legislation, in concert with a number of other countries, will make it possible to have the way of getting at Third World countries that are in arrears to the IMF without having to kick them out of the organization entirely.
To suspend the voting rights of a member within the IMF is a penalty which I certainly hope will not be applied except in the most serious and in the most irresponsible of cases in which a country blatantly refuses to make any efforts whatsoever to put itself into a position of starting to deal with some of its IMF arrears. This bill does make it possible to take such action regardless of what the circumstances are of the arrears which exist.
This is, as the previous speaker noted, a technical bill. I want to just bring it down to earth, if I can, for members of the House and to tell them a little bit about one of the countries that I worked quite closely with in Africa when I worked for the International Development Research Centre before becoming a member of Parliament.
That country is Zambia. It is a country which got itself into serious debt problems not because of anything it did itself, but because of a catastrophic drop in the price of copper. Zambia, in fact, had been a country which had developed fairly sophisticated methods of planning for the future, five-year plans which were aimed to program out quite carefully the new development projects which the country wanted to cany forward.
It was also a country which had recognized that to carry this kind of development forward, it had to put into effect a very strong support policy for individualized agriculture in the country. In fact, one of the things which the IDRC worked on was support for some of these projects with peasant agriculture in Zambia.
I could go on in more detail about Zambia, but I will spare the House that. This is a country which has done a great deal to try to deal with its economic problems. Despite that, because of the tremendous decrease in the price of copper, it found that loans it had taken out for development projects, which looked perfectly viable at the time it took out those loans, suddenly became next to impossible to pay back because there were no longer the export revenues from copper which had seemed to be there in the past.
The consequence for the people of Zambia was that in order to try to pay off some of these loans, it became necessary for the Government of Zambia to massively reduce social programs, to cut back on educational expenditures, on health care, and to significantly reduce the wages of copper workers, for instance, producing the exports of the country.
In short, life for the average person in Zambia became very much harder as a consequence of having to pay back these loans which had been incurred in the past.
We recognize that in the case of many of our aid loans to developing countries, when circumstances like that come up, it makes sense to forgive those loans, to let the country move ahead and therefore to be able to purchase goods from us and purchase goods from other countries in the world.
In the case of commercial loans, however, that is not possible. In the case of bank loans it is not possible. In the case of IMF loans it is generally not something which the IMF permits. Unfortunately, that results in considerable pain and suffering for the people in the country involved.
Some of these countries affected probably have been guilty of irresponsible policies which are very difficult to justify. Panama, for instance, is a country which was not careful in the kinds of development projects it put into effect.
February 25, 1991

One might make the same case for Cambodia and Peru and, perhaps, for a number of other countries such as Zambia, Sudan, Sierra Leone and Costa Rica. These are countries which have generally tried to follow sensible development patterns and yet have found themselves, because of changes in commodity prices-coffee in the case of Costa Rica-unable to pay their debt. I have mentioned copper in the case of Zambia; cocoa in the case of Sierra Leone. These countries faced problems, not because of anything they had or had not done, but because of changes in the world economy.
Mr. Speaker, our hope would be that the IMF will approach such countries with a sense of understanding and a sense of care for the human costs which a tough application of the kinds of policies that lie behind the increased sanctions in this act represent.
I would hope that such a sensitive approach will be taken by the IMF. It is on that basis that we are prepared to see this legislation go forward.
We are not, however, prepared to support this legislation. Despite the useful steps in increasing the amount of money which will be available for Third World countries, the establishment of these new sanctions against such Third World countries represents a negative step which we feel is something the IMF should not be taking and which we are not prepared to support as a party.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to expand further on the question I asked the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans on December 17, 1990 regarding the individual transferable quota system his department planned to implement for Scotia-Fundy. I say "planned" because today it is being implemented for the Scotia-Fundy inshore fishery.
In answer to my question, the minister said on that day that the draggermen of that area have been asking for it, have been asking for individual transferable quotas.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know of any dragger fishermen in the area, small or large dragger fishermen, C-ls or C-2s, who have actually asked for an individual transferable quota. And I will speak more on that. They may have asked for a viable quota, at least a quota that would give them their livelihood.

February 25, 1991
Adjournment Debate
The minister, in my opinion, has not had the decency, the courage or the political will to meet with the fishermen in Nova Scotia, particularly the inshore fishermen, whether in Ottawa or in Nova Scotia. He will always meet with big company officials who come to Ottawa, and I do not want to question why he meets with the larger companies and not the many hundreds of people who are connected with the inshore fishery.
As well, I do not know what his officials have been telling him, but judging from my meetings and the mail, they certainly did not bother to consult with the inshore fishermen of Nova Scotia. The minister may have the Hache task force that he can refer to, but Mr. Hache and his officials did not do the two important things that the fishermen were looking for when they went around: one, evaluating the present stocks before going ahead with their idea of cutting back in the inshore without looking at the actual stock evaluation in those waters; and, two, providing a viable quota. I stress the word viable because this minister is not doing that.
At every meeting I attended and with every letter I received on the subject, it is clear to me that the Scotia-Fundy inshore wants no part of an individual transferable quota, nor any part of the current management plan. You just have to look at the court cases that have been attempted. The dockside grading that the minister wants to implement as it is being looked at in Newfoundland and will come into play after the unemployment scheme for training these people runs out in August, where the individual fishermen, if there are any left, will have to pay for a scheme, that this minister allows, where the fishermen has to report she hours before he can dock and he must report at least two out of the six before he can land, storm or no storm.
It is ridiculous. The minister has forgotten that the markets will not take a good quality fish, that they have individual quotas, that they can report what they have caught, but to continue this system of forcing fishermen and processors to abide by dockside grading and paying for it is ridiculous.
Because of this great management plan we now have National Sea and other large companies transferring their enterprise allocation to smaller boats-which are
more efficient and who used to catch that fish because the offshore could never catch it in the Bay of Fundy and in other areas of the inshore fishery-and we have the large companies asking the under 65-foot dragger fishermen to now fish for them at a reduced price, half the price for the fish, and that fish is then transferred to the offshore companies' plants. That fish used to go into the inshore communities.
That alone should tell the minister that the inshore communities want to meet with him. I would like to have an opportunity to meet with him. In all the time I have been a member of Parliament, whether I was on the government side or the opposition side, I have at least been able or been given the respect in an answer to a letter or a request or whatever to meet with any minister in the House. I have at least been given that. I have waited almost two and half months for a reply to a letter seeking a meeting with the minister on friendly terms, just to talk about the disaster his policy is having. But no, you have to be a big company in order to rate this government or that minister's attention.
I want to tell you what the individual transfer quota will do. This is perhaps the last step in my mind of privatizing a once common resource. It used to be that if you put a quota on, they could go out and fish it. But the result of this transferability is going to be to squeeze out the small owner-operators. Some local industry representatives estimate that the individual transferable quota will result in the loss of one-half of the current employment when the fighting and transfers are finished. I venture to say that you will see with the transferability one to five companies controlling all the catch in the inshore fishery at the end of this management scheme unless this minister is stopped.
I want to say one last thing. It is about the appeal process to this management scheme.
The fishermen got a four-page letter last July 23 and they were given one month to appeal it. What did they have to do?
I think it is almost against human rights. "For a review of catch history, use package A attached." There was package B, too. I think it was 25 pages. "Complete the cover page and Ihble 1, Table 2, Table 3 for any year's landing you wish to contest, and sign the statement
February 25, 1991

confirming data accuracy." The fishermen needed an accountant.
They needed all that in the middle of summer at the time when they were supposed to be fishing, when accountants are on vacation. But they had one month. Supporting documentation was required for the information contained in the tables. This is an affront to any Canadian.
For people who have been in the fishery for 10, 20 or 40 years, documentation must include the following: copies of the buyers' purchase slips, copies of fishing logs, a signed permission form for release of income tax documents to DFO, a signed permission form for release of UIC documents to DFO. This minister is a lawyer. He should realize that is an affront. Any cases of suspected fraud in a letter will be referred to the RCMP.
Now, you tell me that this government is playing fair with the livelihood of the inshore. I know the parliamentary secretary is going to say something on behalf of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans but I think she should tell the minister that if only he would come to meet the fishermen, he would know what is going on, rather than listening to one or two of his officials.
