speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are difficult decisions faced in the 1991 Atlantic Groundfish Management Plan and these were made only after careful consideration of the advice and views provided by the organizations, by fishermen and industry members and provincial governments as well as by fishery scientists who gather and analyse the vital biological data on the various fish stocks, including those of Scotia-Fundy region.
A reasonable balance has been achieved between the conservation of the resource and stability for the participants in the industry and for the economy of the Atlantic region of Canada. The new multi-year approach to managing the groundfish fishery will allow for better planning of Atlantic Canada's groundfish industry and allow Canadian exporters and their customers to develop long-term planning as fish stocks are rebuilt.
Adjournment Debate
The multi-year plan establishes three-year quotas for most groundfish stocks. These TACS will be reviewed by scientists on an ongoing basis and they will be revised should scientific evidence warrant this.
The 1991 plan particularly helps cod fishermen in South West Nova where the quota has been increased to
26,000	tonnes. Furthermore, both inshore draggers and fixed-gear fishermen within the Scotia-Fundy region are better off this year than last. Therefore, the plan will help maintain and provide for long-term stability.
As for the introduction of ITQs for various fisheries, this plan was announced months ago on May 7, 1990, as part of the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program. Where it is deemed feasible and after thorough consultation with affected fishermen, the individual transfer quota systems would be extended to more and more fishermen.
In 1989, over 40 per cent of landings on the Atlantic coast were from vessels operating under the ITQs. The stated plan is thus a reflection of a process which started in the early 1980s in the offshore groundfish fisheries.
Today, all offshore fisheries are under the same type of ITQ and a similar system has recently been extended to smaller vessels in the Gulf and Scotia-Fundy inshore groundfish fisheries. Discussions are ongoing with industry and provincial governments for the introduction of ITQs on the Gulf shrimp fleet.
It is important to notice that the ITQ systems do not entail the privatization of the fishery. Indeed, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans retains his authority to vary these quotas subject to conservation and socioeconomic needs. All transfers of quota between participants require authorization from DFO in the form of amendments to fishing licences.
The introduction of ITQs is a management approach in line with current realities.
Individual allocations allow fishermen to better plan their annual fishing operations and to operate more as business enterprises.

Mr. Speaker, this late show debate involves the question

February 25, 1991
Adjournment Debate
that occurred some time ago in the House on the matter at Oka and a request from our side of the House of the Minister of Justice to implement a public inquiry into the matter at Oka.
I would like to explain why it is absolutely critical that a public inquiry go ahead rather than the partisan, locked-hom relationship of the committee which I really do not think will elucidate the kinds of things Canadians have to know.
In the fall of 1989, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development said he had an agreement in principle with the Mohawks at Kanesatake over the land settlement issue which led to the Oka crisis. In fact, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development had no agreement. The minister submitted a document which he claimed was an agreement in principle, but the document was in fact only signed by three officials of the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs and no one else. It was not an agreement.
The minister claimed that the Mohawk leadership was unable to produce an agreement because it was so badly divided, but in fact the Mohawk leadership had absolutely and unanimously rejected this minister's proposal for an agreement. It is interesting. If the minister is telling the truth he should submit that document to the House of Commons forthwith.
The second matter was that in the spring of 1990, the minister said that he was willing to purchase the lands at Oka, the lands in dispute, and thereby resolve the matter at hand. The Mohawk leadership has a tape of a meeting with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on June 21,1990. On that tape the minister says that he cannot purchase the land because there is no money in the Treasury.
If the minister is telling the truth, he should forthwith lay all documents related to the purchase of those lands before the Oka crisis before the House of Commons.
Every opportunity to resolve this dispute was in the hands of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It involved lands that the municipality at Oka had paid less than $200,000 for. The stupid and incompetent bungling of this issue had to be resolved with 4,000 members of the Canadian Armed Forces faced off against the Mohawk Band at Kanesatake. The stupidity and incompetence of the handling of this issue resulted in a $200 million bill to the Canadian taxpayers
and the Canadian taxpayers are still paying as this process evolves.
We should not be here demanding a public inquiry, which is the only way that we can get the truth from the government and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development by having a judge who can compel witnesses to attend and compel witnesses to testify and produce the documents involved.
These are things that neither this House nor the committee will ever see both because of the lack of power and the lack of determination of the government to bring this matter before the people. We need that public inquiry if Canadians are ever going to see a true version of what happened in the lead-up to the turning loose of 4,000 members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the spending of $200 million in taxpayers' money.
What should really happen is that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development should resign immediately because of the absolute lack of credibility in the contradictory statements put forward by the minister in this House. What the minister's statement contradicts is the truth.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has once again raised the question of a need to call a further inquiry into the stand-off at Oka. The Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs in fact has voted to conduct a comprehensive and independent inquiry into the events of the summer of 1990. The committee will be inviting members of the public who wish to comment on these events to contact it.
This will give those interested an opportunity to discuss fully their concerns and will assist in achieving a full review of the events at Oka and Kahnawake.
To date, there has been substantial review of the events at Oka including an inquiry by the province of Quebec under the National Defence Act and the conclusion by the Federal Court of Canada on two separate occasions that the actions of the forces did not result in any violations of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I am confident that the report of the standing committee will support these earlier findings. However, I welcome the decision of the committee to conduct its inquiry, as I believe this forum will present Canadians
February 25, 1991

with sufficient opportunity to air concerns and access the type of information they may be seeking.
It will also provide answers to questions which may be outstanding. I strongly believe, though, that while we can learn from the past we must look ahead and apply that knowledge to the future for the benefit of all Canadians.
This is the objective of the government's new agenda for aboriginal peoples outlined by the Prime Minister in his speech to this House on September 25, 1990. In that speech, the Prime Minister spoke of an agenda with four main pillars: land claims, economic and social conditions on reserves, the relationship between aboriginal peoples and governments, and concerns of Canada's aboriginal peoples in contemporary Canadian life.
The goal of the agenda is the creation of a new relationship between aboriginal and non-aboriginal Canadians. Defining and developing this relationship will take creativity and perseverance, the courage to see things as they are, the honesty to acknowledge them for what they have become, and the common resolve to correct current problems for the benefit of future generations.
The success of the agenda depends on the commitment and leadership of governments and aboriginal leaders. I am confident that by working together, while looking to the future and applying the lessons of the past, we can achieve the goals of the agenda.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to bring to the attention of the House the sad demise of Winnipeg's Core Area Initiative. This program was begun 10 years ago under the leadership of the member for Winnipeg South Centre who, in his capacity as a minister, brought together the three levels of government work concerned about the future of Winnipeg's inner city.
Up to that point, there had been a great deal of division among these three governments as to what to do with important issues such as the CP rail tracks.
Under the leadership of the Liberal government at that time, a $100 million program was put together which was then renewed and changed in 1985-86. This program is now being left to hang in the air and Winnipegers
Adjournment Debate
would very much like to know the intention of this government.
There are rumours that there will be a one-year extension with no funding. I would like to say to this House that is totally unacceptable to people in the inner city.
Since rumours began to circulate last year that the Core Area Initiative was not going to be renewed, several groups have been meeting in the inner city to discuss the implications of this issue.
The Urban Futures Group, under the leadership of an academic from the University of Winnipeg, presented to the federal and provincial governments several proposals to change the core initiative and to give some 90 groups from the inner city a chance to speak out.
I attended these meetings and I can assure the House that there is a wide range of opinion from both the social activists and the business community seeking to restore the Core Area Initiative to its proper role as a focus for public action in the inner city.
Subsequently, governments refused to meet with this group and its program has been put on the back-burner. Last week, Inner City Voice, a well-known local community newspaper in the inner city, put together another group to discuss these issues.
At that meeting which I attended, many people brought out issues such as housing, the poor condition of housing in the inner city of Winnipeg caused in large part by the refusal of CMHC under this government to fund properly co-op and low income housing. It has left one block after another looking devastated.
In addition, when people do want to renovate their homes, the moneys are no available because the Core Area Initiative has run out of funds.
Second, people talked about day care. We hear a lot from this government about jobs, jobs, jobs; get out, work and look after yourself. Mr. Speaker, you can imagine a situation in which most people who are single parents cannot find the support through day care in order to get into the work force. This government has turned its back.
There was a wonderful program, Parent-Child Centres, in the inner city. It was low cost. There was no bureaucracy attached to it. It involved a few parents getting together in a very simple storefront operation. This government through the Core Area Initiative, could not see its way to continue support. As a result, all these small infrastructures are being taken away. Another organization on Broadway Avenue in the inner city, the

February 25, 1991
Adjournment Debate
West Broadway Family Centre, had a parent respite centre where people could drop in and talk about their problems, talk about the difficulty of bringing up a family alone. That, too, has been taken away.
Everyone in Winnipeg agrees that perhaps North Main is one of the most devastated urban areas in this country. It reminds us in our worst dreams of what it must be like to live in the inner core of an American city.
The North Main Development Corporation, a group of business people, have bravely tried to put together an organization for the last five years in order to build up public support for new facilities, for new infrastructure, to change the impression that only derelict hotels and run down businesses are there, and to tiy to enhance the value of their properties.
One would think that such a conservative agenda would appeal to this government. That the very least they would do is say: "Yes, let us work on North Main". But, no, the only response is a deafening silence that will not help out North Main.
Or perhaps take a look at the CP station, which is one of the most historic sites in Winnipeg. Very responsible leaders in the aboriginal and business community have come forward with a very well thought out program to purchase that building. CP is interested in making a deal. They need one government to take the initiative, to step forward and say: "We will be first in". Then the others would follow.
The Core Area Initiative was designed to help such people get started. Without the core there is no one around to say: "We will give you that extra push to make sure your program takes place."
Again we find that the absence of an active federal government is having devastating results in the inner city.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on with several other examples of how, in the last ten years, the core has become an essential feature in Winnipeg despite some very subtle errors in judgment, such as the way it has become involved with the Forks, or the way it has become involved in the North Portage development site. But the essential idea is to have a concerted effort in the centre
part of a city under tremendous economic stress and to put in a large chunk of money and to have something visible, something that would help out new Canadians, the unemployed, that will train aboriginal youth. A program like that is essential for the future of the city.
This government has ignored Winnipeg when month after month, we have needed government action, a symbol of reassurance that it in fact is committed. We need assurance that the federal government will not pull out of the core as it did out of federal-provincial relations or economic and regional development agreements, that it will not pull out like it did in major industrial projects, that in fact it understands Winnipeg.
We have asked and asked again in the House and there has been nothing but silence. So I ask this government one more time: will they not support the Core Area Initiative, sign a new agreement, show some life, show some support for the centre part of Winnipeg?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the member for Winnipeg North Centre has noted, the Winnipeg core area initiative was created in 1981 under the umbrella of the Canada-Manitoba General Development Agreement in order to respond to what was then a decline in the inner city. This was having an impact on the whole province because the population of Winnipeg is 62.5 per cent of the province of Manitoba.
By 1986 after the expiration of the first five-year agreement considerable strides had been made in reversing that decline and the momentum at that particular time was deemed as just too recent and perhaps too fragile for a withdrawal of public support.
Therefore, as the hon. member has suggested a second agreement under this government was negotiated in 1986 and the five-year economic and general development program was put into place.
Core II, as the program was called, was designed to solidify the momentum and ensure that the trend toward renewed investor confidence was consolidated. That has happened. A brand new 33-storey Toronto-Dominion Centre on the comer of Portage and Main, for example, stands as a testimony to the idea that investor confidence has been renewed in the inner city.
February 25, 1991

All governments have an obligation to ensure that public funding is directed toward the highest priorities, that it responds to current situations and needs, and that it relates directly to mandates of certain areas of government.
Many of the needs of the inner city of Winnipeg, to which the member has referred, fall most appropriately within the mandate of the city and the province. Even so, Winnipeg itself is looking ahead and beyond the inner city. It has shown excellent initiative in establishing Winnipeg 2000 to provide a focal point for economic development for the entire city, economic development, Mr. Speaker, led by the private sector.
What has emerged from this is a renewed sense that the real long-term solution to inner city needs is to increase job opportunities through private sector investment in the city. So whether we achieve this by way of a new tripartite agreement or something different, remains to be negotiated.
However, I will say that Ottawa is not on the verge of abandoning either Winnipeg or Manitoba.
In the health care sector, as an example, some $200 million of investments will be made in Winnipeg and Manitoba and these will include the federal government's virology lab which will be located in the inner city and will have a significant impact on Winnipeg's econo-
Adjoumment Debate
my. Canada is committed to co-operating in areas of federal mandate, whether that will involve formal agreements or simply co-ordination of program areas, it is a little too soon to say.
However, the objectives of Winnipeg 2000 which include the priority emphasis on urban natives as well as on general economic development throughout the city are very much the objectives of my government.
With the private sector, as well as with the municipal and provincial governments, we are moving together in advancing the diversification and industrial development of Winnipeg and of Manitoba as well as focusing the needs on people such as in the native community.
We believe that our directions are those which will have the greatest long-term impact for the community and for the 1990s.
It is with this in mind that the Hon. Jake Epp met with the provincial and municipal counterparts and will be meeting again to discuss an era of new intergovernmental and private sector co-operation for the 1990s.
